nodes.name: DG32-LITE AI Compute Envelope (No Accelerator)
nodes.communityName: 30 Industrial Edge AI Use Cases & Scalar DSP
nodes.description: Physical execution envelope for lightweight edge AI on a 50 MHz RV32IM scalar core. DG32-LITE executes machine learning tasks without an attention engine using a proven scalar hierarchy: 12.5 MMAC/s throughput, 16.5 KB model budget, 82% free CPU cycles, and CORDIC hardware math.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator (Sept 2026) — Slide 01 & 03

nodes.name: Thirty Industrial Use Cases on Scalar Core
nodes.communityName: 30 Industrial Edge AI Use Cases & Scalar DSP
nodes.description: Comprehensive catalogue of 30 predictive diagnostics and control tasks running on DG32-LITE. Four groups of industrial AI workloads that run natively on DG32-LITE without an attention engine, spanning rotating machinery, electrical motor current signature analysis, real-time control, and long-term degradation.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slides 05–10

nodes.name: Tree Ensembles & The 19-Model Hierarchy
nodes.communityName: 30 Industrial Edge AI Use Cases & Scalar DSP
nodes.description: Why zero-multiply decision trees and linear models outperform deep neural networks on microcontrollers. On a scalar CPU without a MAC array, comparisons and table lookups cost almost nothing. A 100-tree random forest at depth 8 requires roughly 800 comparisons and zero multiplications, running in 0.06 ms at >1 kHz.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slides 04–05

nodes.name: Feature Extraction & CORDIC Demodulation
nodes.communityName: 30 Industrial Edge AI Use Cases & Scalar DSP
nodes.description: Costed signal-processing front-end: envelope demodulation, Goertzel filters, and kurtosis rules. The diagnostic front-end reuses CORDIC hardware already present for motor control (Park/Clarke/magnitude/atan2 in <20 cycles). Demodulated features evaluated at known physical fault frequencies outrank raw moments by 4–5×.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slide 06

nodes.name: AFE Sensing Constraints & ISO Standards
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Why the analog front end, not compute or RAM, is the true binding constraint in motor diagnostics. ISO 13373-2 defines usable dynamic range as D = 6(N-1) dB. For an 8-bit ADC, dynamic range is only 42 dB, while broken rotor bar sidebands sit -40 to -60 dBc below the fundamental, disappearing under the quantization floor.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slide 11

nodes.name: CWRU Benchmark Audit & Advisory ML Boundary
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Academic data leakage audit and the strict advisory role of machine learning under hardware lockstep. A critical audit of academic bearing benchmarks reveals widespread data leakage: 40 of 41 published CWRU studies used leaky splits. Furthermore, ML inference on DG32-LITE operates in an advisory role only, subservient to the lockstep safety core.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slide 12

nodes.name: DG32-LITE Lockstep RISC-V MCU
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Dual-core hardware lockstep motor-control SoC for entry-level brushless drives. DG32-LITE puts a RISC-V MCU, motor-control peripherals and a hardware lockstep safety monitor on one 130 nm chip. First silicon rides the September 2026 shuttle.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Datasheet v1.0 & dr.deepgridsemi.com

nodes.name: DG32-2DOM Edge Attention SoC
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Dual-core lockstep motor-control SoC plus isolated INT8 attention engine. The identical frozen control core, pinout and limits as DG32-LITE, with an added INT8 attention engine on its own 114 MHz domain for in-situ bearing anomaly and vibration diagnosis.
nodes.citation: DG32-2DOM Technical Specification & Library Deck

nodes.name: SKU-1: BLDC Motor Controller
nodes.description: High-voltage mixed-signal motor drive with FOC CORDIC hardware accelerator. High-voltage BCD motor controller integrating gate pre-drivers directly onto the chip, achieving <1 µs closed current loop latency with integrated bootstrap diodes.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 2: SKU-1 BLDC Motor

nodes.name: SKU-2: Smart-Meter SoC
nodes.description: Tamper-proof metrology SoC for the 250M National Smart Meter rollout. Dedicated 3-phase and single-phase energy measurement SoC featuring high-dynamic-range 24-bit Sigma-Delta ADCs and hardware tamper detection active even when unpowered.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 3: SKU-2 Smart Meter

nodes.name: SKU-3: Hi-Rel PMIC
nodes.description: Radiation-tolerant power management IC for defense and aerospace avionics. High-reliability power management IC capable of surviving 100V transients on 28V military avionics buses, featuring Brokaw bandgap references and DICE flip-flop state machines.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 4: SKU-3 Hi-Rel PMIC

nodes.name: SKU-4: Lockstep Safety MCU
nodes.description: ASIL-D / SIL-3 functional safety MCU with dual temporally skewed cores. Dual DGridRiscV core microcontroller with 2-clock-cycle temporal skew and spatial separation to eliminate common-cause transient faults and guarantee fail-safe behavior.

nodes.name: SKU-5: Robust Interface Transceiver
nodes.description: Galvanically isolated CAN-FD & RS-485 transceiver for harsh industrial buses. Rugged bus interface transceiver engineered to survive continuous electrical overstress, ground potential differences, and electromagnetic discharge on vehicular harnesses.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 6: SKU-5 Transceiver

nodes.name: SKU-6: Quad-Rail Voltage Supervisor
nodes.description: Ultra-low-jitter precision supply monitor and brownout watchtower. Autonomous analog watchdog that monitors four independent power rails simultaneously, executing clean deglitched reset generation during power brownouts.

nodes.name: SKU-7: 77 GHz 4D MIMO Radar
nodes.description: High-resolution imaging radar front-end in Silicon-Germanium BiCMOS. Sovereign 4D imaging radar RF front-end combining 3 transmitter and 4 receiver channels with integrated fractional-N PLL synthesizer, resolving azimuth and elevation at 3.75 cm range accuracy.

nodes.name: SKU-8: Rugged Display Driver & TCON

nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 9: SKU-8 Display Driver

nodes.name: SKU-9: SDV Zonal Gateway

nodes.description: OpenFrame 2,900 µm wrapper geometric floorplan trade-off: 3×6 vs 3×7 SRAM macro array. Separates the firmware memory footprint question from the physical floorplan question. Moving from 16 to 14 macros in dual-domain 2DOM reduces the grid from 3×7 to 3×6, deleting an entire macro row and expanding the full-width logic strip from 1.75 mm² to 3.40 mm².

nodes.name: DG32-2DOM Dual-Domain System Architecture (CI2612)
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Dual-clock SoC architecture: 50 MHz lockstep flight-control core + 114 MHz attention engine. The DG32-2DOM (A3) combines the hardened DG32-LITE motor-control core with an INT8 attention engine on a second clock, connected through 4-phase CDC level bridges on a 15.30 mm² die.

nodes.name: Hardware INT8 Attention Engine & 40-Bit Numerator (dgrid_int8_attn)

nodes.description: Hardware transformer attention engine with u15 softmax exponential and 40-bit accumulator. Accelerates multi-head self-attention and cross-attention without stalling the CPU domain. Eliminates INT4 quantization collapse by maintaining weights in u15 all the way into a 40-bit signed numerator seat.

nodes.name: AVIP Multimodal Classifier & Stator Current Signature Analysis (CSA)
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL

nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Autonomous multi-stage bootloader: 115200 8N1 banner, 0xD632_B007 flash detection, and SRAM copy. The DG32 architecture operates without an external management core. At power-on, the baked 64 KB std-cell boot ROM executes autonomously, emits console telemetry, verifies flash header magic 0xD632_B007, copies executable code to SRAM, and jumps to application code.

chunks.text: DG32-LITE - Preliminary Datasheet Deepgrid Semi Pvt Ltd - preliminary, confidential Page 1 DEEPGRID SEMI PVT LTD - PRELIMINARY DATASHEET DG32-LITE - Preliminary Datasheet Lockstep RISC-V motor-control SoC on SkyWater sky130A, in a 64-pin QFN. Dual rv32imc cores with a fault comparator, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB self-boot ROM and QSPI-XIP, a 3-phase motor peripheral set (PWM, DShot, encoder, CORDIC, on-die SAR ADC) and UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO. For firmware and hardware/PCB engineers. Part Package Process Core Clock DG32-LITE QFN-64, 9x9 mm sky130A 130 nm 2x rv32imc lockstep 50 MHz Preliminary, pre-silicon. Functional and register detail is from the taped-out RTL and the hardened die. Electrical limits are design targets and sky130 process nominals pending first-silicon characterisation, and are marked where they are not yet measured. The flight-control core is frozen until silicon test. 1 Features • Dual DGridRiscV rv32imc cores in lockstep with a cycle-by-cycle fault comparator and a sticky fault CSR. • 32 KB on-chip SRAM (no ECC); 64 KB baked boot ROM; QSPI execute-in-place window for external NOR flash. • 3-phase center-aligned complementary PWM with programmable dead-time and a hardware brake. • 4-channel DShot ESC engine, pin-muxed onto the PWM output pads. • Quadrature + Hall encoder with edge timestamps; CORDIC (sin/cos, atan2, magnitude) for field-oriented control. • On-die 8-bit differential SAR ADC for phase-current feedback, PWM-triggered. • Two UARTs, an SPI master, a 7-bit I2C master, 14-pin GPIO, two timers, a windowed watchdog and rail supervisor. • Interrupt controller; standalone self-boot (no management core); SLVERR on any unmapped access. • Single 50 MHz clock domain; whole die powered from a 1.8 V rail; 3.3 V I/O. 2 Pinout - 64-pin QFN (top view)

DG32-LITE - Preliminary Datasheet Deepgrid Semi Pvt Ltd - preliminary, confidential Page 6 6 Clock, reset and boot 6.1 Clock and reset A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be used, pull the unused one high. The DG32-LITE die runs entirely from this one 50 MHz domain. 6.2 Boot flow The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help: • Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz). • Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length). • Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2). • Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM. • A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable. Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

DG32-LITE - Preliminary Datasheet Deepgrid Semi Pvt Ltd - preliminary, confidential Page 12 9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB) • Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low. • Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the centre-aligned current-ripple null. • Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V. • SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers into that window and keep the pair matched and short. • QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works. Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor. • I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V). • Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry. • FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor for a hardware trip. • Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers. The flight-control core is frozen until silicon test. 1 Features • Everything in DG32-LITE: dual rv32imc lockstep core, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB boot ROM, QSPI-XIP, and the full motor peripheral set (PWM, DShot, encoder, CORDIC, SAR ADC) plus UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO. • INT8 attention accelerator (0xE000_0000): one kick computes a band of query rows of one head end to end (QK^T, softmax/EXP, E.V, requantise to int8), bit-exact to the golden model. • Attention datapath: shared LANES-wide MAC array, 256-entry u15 EXP table, 40-bit numerator (exact to NK=131072), one reciprocal per row; ~3242 cycles/row analytic at LANES=16. • Second clock domain: the engine runs on clk_fast_i (114 MHz) and crosses to the 50 MHz CPU domain through 2-flop CDC bridges, so it never stalls the frozen control core. • Own die (3400 x 4500 um) with the attention K/V buffers on sky130 SRAM macros next to the SAR analog corner. 2 Pinout - 64-pin QFN (top view)

There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be used, pull the unused one high. DG32-2DOM adds a second clock, clk_fast_i (114 MHz), for the attention engine; the CPU and all peripherals stay in the 50 MHz domain and the two are bridged by CDC logic. 6.2 Boot flow The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help: • Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz). • Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length). • Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2). • Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM. • A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable. Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

DG32-2DOM adds a second clock, clk_fast_i (114 MHz), for the attention engine; the CPU and all peripherals stay in the 50 MHz domain and the two are bridged by CDC logic. 6.2 Boot flow The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help: • Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz). • Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length). • Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2). • Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM. • A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable. Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

DG32-2DOM - System Architecture Deepgrid Semi Pvt Ltd - confidential Page 24 11 Application: AVIP bearing-fault detection The DG32-2DOM attention engine exists to run models like AVIP, an INT8 bearing-fault classifier (dgrid-a8w8). AVIP is multimodal - a time branch and an FFT branch, each a small conv stack plus a gated recurrent cell - fused by two self-attention blocks and one cross-attention block, ending in a per-class head. Those attention blocks are exactly what the engine accelerates. The shipped CWRU-trained model is 47,076 parameters at 94-95% held-out-load accuracy with INT8 equal to FP32; the full AVIP topology is 478,277 parameters. Both map onto the same op set with no new RTL. 11.1 What runs on the attention engine Model stage What it is DG32-2DOM mapping Self-attention (sa, sb) QKV projection + softmax(QK^T)V per head K_ATTN -> dgrid_int8_attn Cross-attention (cx) time<->freq fusion, one head set K_ATTN -> dgrid_int8_attn Head dimension key_dim 16 -> KD=16 multiple of LANES=16, within KDMAX=32 - fits as built Kicks per inference 6 (CWRU model) / 12 (full AVIP) one kick per (window, head) Conv / elementwise / dense the rest of the graph K_CONV / K_ELEM / K_AGEMM on the INT8 tile 11.2 Inference budget (measured on the INT8 op-graph) Model Positions Kicks Conv cycles Time (ms) CWRU model (47K params) 143,377 228,229 3,794,371 46.7 Full AVIP (478K params) 169,821 231,657 4,429,355 54.5 AVIP has 10x the parameters but only 1.2x the compute: its capacity is in deeper, narrower layers at lower spatial resolution, and compute tracks positions, not parameter count. The engine runs on clk_fast_i, so the ~50 ms inference does not steal cycles from the 50 MHz control core. Footprint.

The AVIP arena is ~2.49 MB (weights, LUTs, activations), so the full model runs from external memory on the DG32-2DOM / a8w8 class part - not from the 32 KB on-chip SRAM. The on-chip attention engine and INT8 tile are shared; the model image and activations live off-chip. 11.3 Current-signature front end (no accelerometer) AVIP trains on two accelerometers (drive-end + fan-end). A motor-control die already has the sensor it needs: the phase-current SAR ADC. A bearing defect modulates the stator current at f_e +/- k*f_fault (Current Signature Analysis), so the current envelope carries the same fault signature. The front end (fw/avip_csa) samples the SAR ADC at the PWM ripple null, derives two channels from the one current (raw carrier + AM envelope), and produces both a standalone classical fault score and the AVIP INT8 recurrence tensor. Item How Note Sensor On-die SAR ADC (0xDB), PWM-triggered no external accelerometer or vibration probe Channels current + envelope the DE/FE analogue from a single ADC Classical indicator BPFO/BPFI/BSF sideband energy, 0..255 ~9 KB, fits DG32-LITE; runs every window NN input (35,20,20,2) INT8 recurrence tensor streamed to the arena for the op-graph on 2DOM The classical indicator is a usable detector on its own and needs no accelerator, so it also runs on DG32-LITE; the trained-network path adds accuracy on DG32-2DOM. Bearing-fault detection is therefore a concrete reason the attention variant exists, and it reuses the motor's own current sense.

0 2 · A L G O R I T H M C H O I C E Where a scalar core is strong The absence of a MAC array reverses the usual ranking. Comparisons and table lookups cost almost nothing here. Tree ensembles are the best accuracy per cycle on this part A 100-tree random forest at depth 8 is roughly 800 comparisons and no multiplies at all — 0.06 ms, supporting rates above 1 kHz. A neural network of comparable accuracy on bearing-fault or power-quality classification costs 50–500× more cycles. This is not a compromise made for the hardware. On the CWRU bearing benchmark a random forest over five time-domain features reaches 95.6 %, and cutting from nine features to five costs 0.1 %. A review of 42 papers finds SVM at 95–100 % against deep methods at 97–100 % — statistically indistinguishable. Model capacity is not the bottleneck on these tasks. Signal conditioning is. The ordering that follows First choice — tree ensembles, linear discriminants, PCA with Hotelling T², Mahalanobis distance. Sub-millisecond, kHz-capable, inspectable in the field. Second choice — small dense networks and autoencoders, where a nonlinear boundary genuinely earns its place. Still sub-millisecond. Reach for last — recurrent and convolutional models. A GRU at 2.95 ms and a 1D-CNN at 10.3 ms both fit, but only where the raw waveform carries something hand-built features miss. Design rule. Spend effort on band selection, envelope demodulation and operating-condition normalisation before spending it on model capacity. 0 4 · F R O N T E N D Feature extraction, costed Every use case pairs one or two of these with one model. The CORDIC unit does Park, Clarke, magnitude and atan2 in hardware, so the diagnostic front end reuses what the control loop already computes. S T A G E C Y C L E S T I M E W H A T I T Y I E L D S 256-point real FFT 30,720 0.61 ms Band energies, spectral peaks, harmonic ratios 512-point real FFT 69,120 1.38 ms Finer resolution for gear-mesh and sideband work Envelope demodulation 5,000 0.10 ms CORDIC magnitude, 20 iterations — the bearing-fault front end Goertzel, 8 bins 6,144 0.12 ms Narrowband detection at predicted fault frequencies Statistical moments 7,000 0.14 ms RMS, kurtosis, crest factor, skew — ISO 20816 baseline Broadband RMS velocity 3,000 0.06 ms ISO 20816 severity zone A/B/C/D Haar wavelet, 256 samples 15,000 0.30 ms Time-frequency features for transient faults Park / Clarke transform 120 0.00 ms CORDIC, already computed by the control loop Decimation and band- pass 4,000 0.08 ms IIR biquads ahead of envelope or raw- waveform models Why this matters more than the model A published feature-ranking study across twelve features found demodulated features evaluated at the known fault frequency outrank raw statistical moments by a factor of 4–5. Hilbert-Huang amplitude at the outer-race frequency scored 225.9; peak-to-peak scored 51.8. That is the whole argument for spending cycles on envelope demodulation and band selection rather than on a larger classifier. The envelope chain is also cheap: band-pass, rectify, low-pass, decimate to 1–2 kS/s, then a modest FFT. Do the decimation before buffering and the working set never exceeds a few kB. One caution.

Kurtosis is non-monotonic — it peaks for incipient localised defects then falls as damage spreads and the signal becomes Gaussian. RMS is the opposite: stable and monotonic, but blind to early faults. Trend both; never alarm on kurtosis alone. 0 9 · C O N S T R A I N T What the sensing supports Compute is not the binding constraint on these thirty use cases. The analog front end is. The current-based use cases need more than 8 bits ISO 13373-2 gives usable dynamic range as D = 6(N−1) dB, so eight bits yields 42 dB. ISO 20958 states rotor-bar sidebands sit 100 to 1,000 times below the fundamental — −40 to −60 dBc. The entire diagnostic range sits at or below the quantisation floor. Broken rotor bar, eccentricity and inter-turn short detection need either analog fundamental suppression and gain ahead of the converter, or 12–16 bits. A second constraint compounds it. Sideband separation is 2·s·f₁ — roughly 3 Hz at full load, 0.5 Hz at light load — so these use cases need 30–100 second records at stable load and speed with 0.01–0.05 Hz resolution. A 2²⁰-point FFT is 8 MB and does not fit. Use Goertzel evaluated at the predicted sideband frequencies, which is why the electrical use cases on slide 06 are costed that way and not with an FFT. Tier 1 — one accelerometer The highest-value addition. Bearings are 44 % of motor failures and are the weakest fault class for current-only sensing; rotor bars, where current is strongest, are 8–10 %. Needs ≥5 kHz usable bandwidth — many low-cost MEMS parts roll off at 1–3 kHz, below the bearing resonance band, which makes envelope analysis useless. Mounting matters as much as the part: stud mounting per ISO 13373-1, not magnet or adhesive. Tier 2 — three-phase current and voltage Unlocks negative-sequence detection of stator inter-turn shorts, instantaneous power signature analysis and Park's vector per ISO 20958 Annex A. Needs a multi-channel converter; the part currently has one differential channel.

What works today, unchanged Everything on slide 08 and most of slide 09 — vibration-based classification, sensorless observation, plausibility checking, regime identification, anomaly scoring and duty tracking — runs on the sensing already present, because they depend on relative change rather than absolute small-signal resolution. A P P E N D I X Basis Read this before quoting any figure elsewhere. From the design Core configuration, memory sizes, peripheral set and the CORDIC capability come from the DG32- LITE block diagrams dated 10 September 2026 and the consolidated capability assessment of 11 September 2026. The 16.5 KB and 29.5 KB model budgets and the 12.5 MMAC/s scalar rate are taken from that assessment. Derived Every latency, memory figure and maximum rate in this deck is calculated — feature- extraction cycles plus model cycles at 4 cycles per int8 multiply-accumulate, against 82 % of a 50 MHz core. That constant is back-solved from the design documents and has not been measured on silicon. One cycle- accurate measurement on run R firmware relocates every rate here. Third-party, verified 11 Sept 2026 CWRU random-forest accuracy and the 42-paper review, the twelve-feature ranking study, the kurtosis non-monotonicity result, and the ISO signal-processing limits were checked against primary sources — IEEE and MDPI papers, the PHM Society proceedings, and the ISO catalogue entries for 13373-1, 13373-2, 20958 and 20816- 3. On accuracy expectations Do not carry published bearing-benchmark accuracy into a specification. Forty of forty-one reviewed CWRU studies used splits vulnerable to data leakage; on a leakage-free bearing-wise split one classifier fell from 85.8 % to 69.5 %. Realistic accuracy on unseen physical bearings is 65–80 %. Smith and Randall further showed a meaningful fraction of CWRU records are not diagnosable by correct physics at all, which is why 99 % figures on that dataset should be treated as artefacts. What is not claimed No workload here has been compiled for or measured on DG32-LITE, which has not completed place-and-route.

No inference result carries a safety integrity claim — that architecture places the classifier in an advisory role with a lockstepped deterministic monitor holding the trip limits. Model choices are the appropriate algorithm for each task on this core, not trained and validated implementations. DG32-LITE - Preliminary Datasheet Deepgrid Semi Pvt Ltd - preliminary, confidential Page 6 6 Clock, reset and boot 6.1 Clock and reset A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be used, pull the unused one high. The DG32-LITE die runs entirely from this one 50 MHz domain. 6.2 Boot flow The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help: • Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz). • Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length). • Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2). • Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM. • A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable. Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor. • I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V). • Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry. • FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor for a hardware trip. • Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers. JTAG idles safely with no probe. TMS (pin 25) and TDI (pin 26) are weakly pulled up on die, TCK (pin 24) weakly pulled down, so an unconnected JTAG header will not disturb the part.

dgrid_dshot_rx — DShot receive + bidirectional telemetry reply Block spec for review · DG32 · 13 Sep 2026 · draft 1 Author: DG32 engineering (drafted with Claude). Reviewer: Ayaz Khan. 0. Ayaz's questions — answered from the RTL # Question Answer Source 1 Do the timers at 0xD4/0xD5 have pin-routed input capture? No. dgrid_timer 's entire non-AXI interface is tick_o and irq_o . No input pin, no capture register. DShot300-via- timer is not an interim path. rtl/dgrid_timer.sv module ports 1b Is there any edge- timestamp hardware on the die? Yes — on the encoder. dgrid_encoder (0xDA) has a free-running 32-bit timestamp_q captured on Hall/quadrature edges ("Hall decode with edge timestamps"). It is functionally input- capture, bonded to the encoder/Hall pads, not the timers. rtl/dgrid_encoder.sv:26,91-95 2 Datasheet says 14 GPIO, pinout bonds 3 — which is right? The pinout. NGPIO = 3 . It was 14; 11 pads were reclaimed for I²C (2) and scan/DFT (4). The datasheet is stale and must be corrected. rtl/dg32_lite_top.sv:149 3 28 KB vs 32 KB SRAM Both positions are legitimate and they answer different questions — see §9. The codex branch is already running both a 24 KB variant ( 2dom/12 ) and a keep-32 KB spread-floorplan test ( 2dom/13 ). Those runs decide it with data. autoresearch/configs/2dom/12,13 4 "DShot bidirectional / RPM telemetry — settled: not supported" Re-opened by this spec. Ayaz's case is correct: it cannot be done in firmware, and it is required for DG32-as-ESC. this document 1. Why firmware cannot do this (confirming Ayaz's argument) DShot600 is 1.67 µs/bit; the 0/1 decision is a high-time of 625 ns vs 1250 ns.

At 50 MHz that is 31 vs 62 cycles, so the decode needs ~±15-cycle (±300 ns) edge placement — achievable only by a busy-wait loop with interrupts off for the full 16-bit frame (~1,340 cycles at DShot600, ~2,700 at DShot300). That collides with: the 5 µs FOC loop (250 cycles) — a single DShot frame is 5× longer than the entire control period;

the lockstep compare window — dgrid_lockstep_check compares every committed store; a firmware bit-bang that branches on pad reads produces store streams whose timing depends on an asynchronous input, which is exactly the class of behaviour the checker is designed to flag. And bidirectional reply is impossible in firmware regardless of speed: the ESC must turn the pad from input to output ~30 µs after the command frame ends and drive a 21-bit reply — the pad has no output-enable today. This is a pad-ring fact, not a software one. Conclusion: hardware RX + hardware reply, or no ESC role. 2. What exists today (baseline) dgrid_dshot (slot 0xC, rtl/dgrid_dshot.sv ) is transmit-only: 4 channels, one shared bit-time counter, per-channel 16-bit frame + CRC4, programmable BITPERIOD / T0H / T1H . Its only pins are output [3:0] dshot_o . The four channels reach the pads only through SYSCTL PINMUX[0] , which AND-ORs them onto the PWM high-side pads AH / BH / CH / SAMPLE_TRIG ( dg32_lite_top.sv:775-792 ). The low-side PWM pads are never muxed, so a mis-set mux cannot shoot through a bridge. Pad budget is 44/44 with zero spare. There is no pad for a receiver. The RX path therefore must reuse the same four pads, which means those pads become bidirectional. That is the single most consequential change in this spec (§7). 3. Protocol facts the design depends on 3.1 Command frame (FC → ESC), what RX decodes 16 bits, MSB first: [15:5] throttle (11 b) · [4] telemetry request · [3:0] CRC4.

Each bit is one pulse of fixed period; high-time encodes the value (long = 1, short = 0). speed bit period T0H T1H @50 MHz period / T0H / T1H (cycles) DShot150 6.67 µs 2.50 µs 5.00 µs 333 / 125 / 250 DShot300 3.33 µs 1.25 µs 2.50 µs 167 / 62 / 125 DShot600 1.67 µs 0.625 µs 1.25 µs 83 / 31 / 62 DShot1200 0.83 µs 0.312 µs 0.625 µs 42 / 16 / 31 CRC4, normal mode: crc = n0 ^ n1 ^ n2 of the 12-bit {throttle, telem} — identical to the TX engine's crc4_of() . CRC4, bidirectional mode: crc = ~(n0 ^ n1 ^ n2) & 0xF . The inverted CRC is how the protocol marks a bidirectional-capable frame. 3.2 Bidirectional mode signalling In bidirectional DShot the line is inverted: idle high, bits are low pulses (high-time above becomes low-time). The ESC recognises bidirectional mode from the inverted idle level and inverted CRC. RX needs an INVERT control bit that flips the input sense before the width measurement.

chunks.section: 3.3 Telemetry reply (ESC → FC), what the reply engine sends
chunks.text: 3.3 Telemetry reply (ESC → FC), what the reply engine sends The reply is not a DShot command frame, so it cannot reuse the TX engine's shifter unmodified: 1. Payload: 16 bits = [15:4] eRPM period (3-bit exponent e , 9-bit mantissa m ; period_µs = m << e ) · [3:0] CRC where crc = ~(v ^ v>>4 ^ v>>8) & 0xF over the 12-bit period field. 2. GCR 4b→5b encode each nibble (table: 19 1B 12 13 1D 15 16 17 1A 09 0A 0B 1E 0D 0E 0F ) → 20 bits. 3. Transition-encode to 21 bits: out[0] = 0; out[i] = out[i-1] ^ G[i-1] — a 1 in the GCR stream is a level transition, not a level. 4. Transmit inverted, at 5/4 the command bit rate (DShot600 → 750 kbit/s, 1.33 µs/bit = 66.7 cycles), starting ~30 µs after the command frame's last edge. The FC decodes edges back with G = s ^ (s >> 1) . This is the Betaflight/Bluejay/AM32 convention; get any of the three steps wrong and every FC on the market reports CRC errors. 4. Architecture Recommendation: extend slot 0xC in place, not a new slot. The RX and reply engines are added inside dgrid_dshot as two self-contained sub-modules ( dgrid_dshot_rx , dgrid_dshot_tel ), sharing the existing AXI slave, the pad mux and the bit-timing registers.

chunks.section: 3.3 Telemetry reply (ESC → FC), what the reply engine sends
chunks.text: Reasons: (a) the address map has no free slot without touching the decoder and error-slave logic that is frozen for tape-in; (b) RX and TX are mutually exclusive on the same pads, so one owner of the pad direction is safer than two; (c) BITPERIOD/T0H/T1H already encode the speed class — RX derives its threshold from them by default. ┌───────────── dgrid_dshot (slot 0xC) ─────────────┐ AXI-lite ──────────►│ regs │ TX engine (existing) ───────────┐ │ │ │ │ mux/dir │──► pad_o[3:0] │ │ dgrid_dshot_tel (reply, GCR) ────┤ + OE │──► pad_oe[3:0] │ │ │ │ │ │ dgrid_dshot_rx ◄── sync/filter ◄┘ │◄── pad_i[3:0] │ └── irq_o │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Per channel (×4): RX decoder, reply shifter, direction FSM. Shared: bit-time counter (existing), threshold/timeout/turnaround registers, 2-FF synchronisers. 4.1 RX decoder (per channel) Input: pad_i → 2-FF synchroniser → 2-sample glitch filter → INVERT XOR → rx_level . Rising edge of rx_level starts a 12-bit high-time counter; falling edge stops it and compares to RXTHRESH : bit = (high_time > RXTHRESH) . 16-bit shift register, MSB first. A 4-bit bit counter completes the frame at 16. Frame boundary: an idle period longer than RXTIMEOUT cycles (default ≈ 2 × BITPERIOD) resets the bit counter — this is how a mid-frame glitch or a lost edge cannot desynchronise the receiver permanently. On 16 bits: compute CRC4 per §3.1 (mode-dependent), latch {throttle, telem} , set VALID ; set CRC_ERR instead if mismatch; set OVERRUN if VALID was still set (firmware hadn't read the previous frame).

Synchroniser + filter add a fixed 3-cycle (60 ns) latency to both edges, so measured width is unaffected. 4.2 Reply engine dgrid_dshot_tel (per channel) Armed when TELEM_EN=1 and a valid frame with telem=1 arrives (or TELEM_ALWAYS=1 — bidirectional FCs expect a reply on every frame). Waits TURNAROUND cycles from the command frame's last edge, then asserts pad_oe , drives the 21-bit stream from TELEMn at TELEMPERIOD cycles/bit (inverted), then releases pad_oe and returns the pad to input. GCR + transition encoding (§3.3) done in hardware from the 12-bit period value firmware writes to TELEMn . Firmware supplies only {e, m} ; CRC, GCR and transition coding are hardware. This keeps the firmware side to one register write per commutation-period update. If a new command frame's first edge arrives while a reply is being driven, the reply is aborted and OE released within one cycle — never fight the FC for the wire. TEL_ABORT status bit is set. 4.3 Direction ownership pad_oe per channel is the OR of: TX engine BUSY (existing TX role, always drives) and dgrid_dshot_tel driving . In RX-only or RX+reply roles the TX engine is never started, so the pad idles as input. PINMUX[0] continues to select DShot vs PWM; PWM-role pads remain output- only (OE forced high) so the bridge-safety property is preserved. 5.

Register map (slot 0xC, addr[7:0] ; existing registers 0x00–0x20 unchanged) addr name bits R/W description 0x24 RXCTRL [0] RX_EN RW enable receivers (all 4 channels) [1] INVERT RW bidirectional-mode sense: idle high, low pulses, inverted CRC [2] TELEM_EN RW reply engine armed on frames with telem bit set [3] TELEM_ALWAYS RW reply on every valid frame regardless of telem bit [4] IRQ_FRAME_EN RW interrupt on any channel VALID [5] IRQ_ERR_EN RW interrupt on any channel CRC_ERR / OVERRUN / TEL_ABORT [7:6] — reserved, read 0 0x28 RXTHRESH [11:0] RW high-time (cycles) above which a bit reads 1. Default (T0H + T1H) / 2 if written 0. 0x2C RXTIMEOUT [11:0] RW idle cycles that terminate/reset a partial frame. Default 2 × BITPERIOD if 0.

addr name bits R/W description 0x30 RXFRAME0 [10:0] THROTTLE RO received throttle, channel 0 [11] TELEM RO telemetry-request bit as received [12] VALID RO/W1C frame received, CRC good. Cleared by writing 1 (see note on why not read-to-clear) [13] CRC_ERR RO/W1C frame received, CRC bad [14] OVERRUN RO/W1C a new frame completed before VALID was cleared [15] TEL_ABORT RO/W1C reply aborted by an incoming command edge 0x34 RXFRAME1 as above channel 1 0x38 RXFRAME2 as above channel 2 0x3C RXFRAME3 as above channel 3 0x40 TURNAROUND [15:0] RW cycles from command frame's last edge to reply start. DShot600 nominal 30 µs = 1500. 0x44 TELEMPERIOD [11:0] RW reply bit period in cycles. Default BITPERIOD × 4 / 5 if 0 (DShot600 → 67). 0x48 TELEM0 [11:0] {e[2:0], m[8:0]} RW eRPM period to reply on channel 0. Hardware appends CRC, GCR- encodes, transition-encodes. 0x4C TELEM1 RW channel 1 0x50 TELEM2 RW channel 2 0x54 TELEM3 RW channel 3 0x58 RXSTATUS [3:0] VALID[ch] · [7:4] CRC_ERR[ch] · [11:8] OVERRUN[ch] · [15:12] TEL_BUSY[ch] · [19:16] PAD_DIR[ch] (1 = driving) RO one-read snapshot of all four channels 0x5C RXIRQ [0] FRAME · [1] ERR RO/W1C interrupt pending flags Reset state: RX_EN=0 , all thresholds 0 (→ derived defaults), all pads input-disabled only if the wrapper's pad config leaves them so — see §7. Note on clearing VALID : W1C is the safe default and matches the other DG32 peripherals. Read-to-clear is not recommended: the lockstep checker mirrors bus reads to the CHECKER core two cycles late, so a read with a side-effect would be observed by both cores but the side-effect happens once — safe in practice, but it is exactly the kind of subtlety the design avoids elsewhere. Keep W1C.

6. Interrupts One new source into dgrid_irq (0xDF): dshot_rx_irq = (IRQ_FRAME_EN & |VALID) | (IRQ_ERR_EN & |(CRC_ERR|OVERRUN|TEL_ABORT)) . Level, cleared by W1C of the underlying flags. dgrid_irq has a 16-bit raw vector with bits 0–6 and 8 (attention, 2dom) used; bit 7 is 1'b0 today and is the natural slot ( rtl/dgrid_irq.sv:58 ). Bits 9–15 are also free. Follow the existing convention: add dshot_rx_i = 1'b0 as a defaulted port so the frozen lite netlist is unchanged when the port is left unconnected — and tie it explicitly in the top (sv2v drops port defaults). 7. Pad-ring change — the real cost of this feature The four DShot pads are io[26] P_PWM_AH , io[28] P_PWM_BH , io[30] P_PWM_CH , io[32] P_PWM_TRIG ( openframe/openframe_project_wrapper.v:134-136 ). Today they are class PC_OUT ( pad_class() at line 470: i >= P_PWM_AH && i <= P_PWM_TRIG ), i.e. gpio_dm = 110 , gpio_inp_dis = 1 , oeb tied to constant drive (lines 408–414). The wrapper already has the class we need: PC_BIDIR ( gpio_dm = 110 , gpio_inp_dis = 0 , oeb dynamic) is what QSPI IO0–3, I²C and the three GPIOs use. So the change is three edits, not a new pad mode: edit today required pad_class() io[26..32] → PC_OUT io[26], io[28], io[30], io[32] → PC_BIDIR ; io[27], io[29], io[31] stay PC_OUT oeb_v[P_PWM_AH/BH/CH/TRIG] gpio_loopback_zero (always drive) ~pad_oe[ch] from dgrid_dshot , through u_glue like gpio3_oeb (oeb is active-low) gpio_in[P_PWM_AH/BH/CH/TRIG] unused → dgrid_dshot.pad_i[3:0] through the top-level gpio_ib_mode_sel , gpio_vtrip_sel , gpio_slow_sel stay at their existing all-zero tie (CMOS input, standard trip) — same as the other bidirectional pads.

Why it still carries risk: the whole per-pad config table rests on an item your tape-in notes flag — the exact gpio_dm / inp_dis encoding was never verified against the real OpenFrame template; TODO in the wrapper header, confirm before GATE-3. Four pads that switch direction at runtime make that verification mandatory. It is the same verification the QSPI and I²C pads need anyway, so this adds no new unknown — it raises the cost of an existing one. Bridge safety is preserved: the low-side pads io[27] AL , io[29] BL , io[31] CL are untouched and remain PC_OUT . When PINMUX[0]=0 (PWM role) pad_oe is forced high for all four muxed pads, so they behave exactly as today. Two more pad-level checks for the reviewer: 1. Idle level. PC_BIDIR ( dm=110 ) has no weak pull — the pull modes ( dm=010/011 ) are input-only classes in this wrapper, and gpio_dm is a static tie, not switchable at runtime. So when the pad is input and the FC is not driving, the line floats. Bidirectional DShot idles high, normal DShot idles low. Recommendation: require the external pull on the board (bidirectional-DShot ESC wiring already puts a pull-up on the FC side) and document it in the datasheet; do not attempt a runtime-switched gpio_dm . 2. Reset. busy_q resets to 0 ( rtl/dgrid_dshot.sv:74 ) and dshot_o to 0, so the TX engine does not drive

out of reset. pad_oe must follow: input during rst_n_i low, so a resetting DG32 never drives a line the FC is driving. Note this inverts the current reset behaviour of these four pads (today they drive 0 out of reset as PC_OUT ) — the board must not rely on a hard low from AH/BH/CH during reset. AL/BL/CL are unchanged. 8. Timing, cost and verification Edge precision at 50 MHz (20 ns/cycle): the decision margin is T1H − T0H . DShot300: 63 cycles (±630 ns) — trivial. DShot600: 31 cycles (±310 ns) — comfortable. DShot1200: 15 cycles (±150 ns) — works on paper, but the synchroniser's ±1-cycle sampling jitter plus FC- side jitter eats a third of it. Recommend DShot600 as the supported maximum; DShot1200 best-effort. Area estimate: per channel — 12-bit width counter, 16-bit RX shifter, 4-bit CRC, RX FSM (~70 flops); 21-bit reply shifter, 12-bit period counter, GCR/transition encoder (~50 flops); status/flags (~8). ×4 ≈ ~520 flops plus shared registers (~100) and 8 synchroniser flops. Roughly 1,500– 2,500 std cells — about 3–5% of the lite die's 50,550. Consistent with Ayaz's "cheap": the TX engine closes at 172.9 MHz against 50 MHz, and RX has no deeper logic. Verification plan (before integration, all standalone): 1. tb_dshot_rx — loopback: existing TX engine drives RX through a modelled pad at all four speeds; every throttle 0–2047 × telem 0/1; assert RXFRAME == transmitted and VALID . Also inject each single-bit corruption → assert CRC_ERR , never VALID . 2. Glitch/desync: inject a 40 ns glitch mid-frame; assert timeout resync and that the next frame decodes clean. 3. Overrun: two frames back-to-back without a read → OVERRUN .

4. tb_dshot_tel — reply stream captured by a reference FC decoder implementing G = s ^ (s>>1) + GCR table + CRC check, written independently from the encoder (not shared code). All 4096 period values. 5. Turnaround: assert pad_oe rises exactly TURNAROUND cycles after the last command edge and falls after bit 21; assert abort-on-incoming-edge releases OE within 1 cycle. 6. Bidirectional end-to-end: FC model sends inverted frame with inverted CRC; RX decodes; reply goes out inverted at 5/4 rate; FC model validates. 7. Integrated: re-run fwtest T- suite (T01–T17) bit-identical, plus a new T18 dshot_rx loopback on the FPGA using a jumper between two DShot pads. Lockstep: RX is a normal bus slave. Its registers are read by MAIN and mirrored to CHECKER like every other peripheral; no store timing depends on the asynchronous input, because decoding is in hardware. This is the property firmware bit-banging cannot provide. 9. SRAM: 28 KB vs 32 KB — separating the two questions Ayaz: "28 KB bare minimum, 32 KB with safety margin; the reusable buffer saves only 2 KB." That is a firmware footprint statement, and it is the right way to size memory. The 28 KB proposal was a floorplan lever: 16 → 14 macros lets 2dom's 17 macros fit 3 columns × 6 rows instead of 3 × 7, deleting an entire macro row and growing the full-width logic strip from 1.75 mm² to 3.40 mm² — that is what makes 2dom fit the 2,900 µm wrapper slot at all. It was never a claim that firmware needs less memory.

Both can be true. The question is whether 2dom can fit at 2,900 µm with 32 KB, and the codex branch is already answering it empirically: 2dom/13 is a keep-32 KB spread-floorplan test, 2dom/12 a 24 KB variant. If 13 routes and closes, keep 32 KB and drop the 28 KB idea. If only the reduced-SRAM variants fit, then the firmware team gets 28 KB and the 2 KB reusable buffer stops being optional. Decide from those two runs, not from either side's estimate. Note the lite die is unaffected either way — it stays 32 KB. 10. What to implement — the list RTL 1. rtl/dgrid_dshot_rx.sv — per-channel RX decoder (§4.1), 4 instances, parameterised on TW=12 . 2. rtl/dgrid_dshot_tel.sv — per-channel GCR/transition reply engine (§4.2). 3. Extend dgrid_dshot.sv : registers 0x24–0x5C (§5), pad_i[3:0] input, pad_oe[3:0] output, irq_o , direction FSM (§4.3). Existing 0x00–0x20 behaviour and the TX engine unchanged; tb_dshot must still pass bit-identical. 4. dg32_lite_top.sv : route pad_i / pad_oe for the four muxed pads; OE forced high in PWM role; new IRQ source into dgrid_irq . Wrapper / pad ring 5. openframe_project_wrapper.v : io[26/28/30/32] PC_OUT → PC_BIDIR in pad_class() ; oeb_v for those four from ~pad_oe via u_glue ; gpio_in for those four to the top; OE deasserted in reset. Board-side pull documented (no on-die pull in this class). 6. Verify the OpenFrame per-pad control encoding against the real template — already a GATE-3 TODO; now blocking. Firmware / docs 7. dg32.h : register defines; fwtest T18 loopback test. 8. Datasheet: GPIO 14 → 3; DShot bidirectional "not supported" → "supported, DShot150–600, best-effort 1200"; document the pad-direction behaviour. 9. DG_lite_analysis.md item 9: reopen. Verification — §8 items 1–7.

Not in scope of this change: a new bus slot (kept at 0xC), timer input capture (not needed once RX is hardware), any change to the low-side PWM pads. 11. Open questions for Ayaz before implementation starts 1. Roles per pad — is DG32 ever both FC (TX) and ESC (RX) on different channels simultaneously? The spec allows it (per-channel direction), but if not required, a global role bit simplifies the FSM. 2. Reply on every frame ( TELEM_ALWAYS ) vs only on telem-request — which FC firmware are you targeting first? Betaflight bidirectional expects every frame. 3. Idle level: the bidirectional pad class has no on-die pull (§7). Is a board-side pull-up acceptable, or do you need the die to define the idle level? (The latter means a runtime- switched gpio_dm , which I recommend against.) 4. Reset behaviour change: AH/BH/CH/TRIG will float (input) during reset instead of driving 0 . Is anything on your board relying on the hard low? 5. Priority vs tape-in: this touches the wrapper's unverified pad config. It is not for the 16 Sep die. Confirm it targets the following shuttle (CI2612) alongside 2dom.

India buys almost every one of its simpler chips from other countries. About $9 billion of them a year. These are the unexciting parts inside every vehicle, electricity meter, drone and defence box: power chips, small processors, motor drivers, data-line chips, voltage monitors. DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL PART ONE India buys almost every one of these chips from abroad Nobody in India makes them. The reason is money, not skill. And money can be changed. 1 What India buys, and why nobody here makes it Start with one number. Last year India imported $23.4 billion of chips. That figure is from UN COMTRADE, code HS 8542. It is the only number in this section that comes from outside our company. About 70 % of it came from China and Taiwan. Inside that total, analysts estimate about $9 billion a year is the kind of chip this document is about. These are chips made on older, larger factory processes — 130 nanometres and above. Power management chips. Small microcontrollers. Motor gate drivers. Data-line transceivers. Voltage supervisors. Electricity- meter front ends. These are not exciting chips. But they are most of the chips in any product. A car has one or two advanced processors and several dozen of these older ones. A smart electricity meter has none of the advanced kind at all. So the import bill is large, and it stays large. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 6
DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 7

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL Figure 1 is a funnel, not a headline. Each step down makes the number smaller and makes it more believable. Walk down it: • $23.4 bn to $9 bn. We cut out chips made on newer, smaller processes. We do not build those. This divides the number by 2.6. • $9 bn to $0.46 bn. We cut down to the nine kinds of chip we actually build. This is the biggest cut, a factor of 19. • $0.46 bn to ₹1,000 Cr. This is what we think we can sell by FY31. • ₹1,000 Cr to ₹2.88 Cr. This is what we have already sold. A factor of 35. We would rather you argue with the bottom number than believe the top one. 1.1 Why has nobody in India filled this gap? India has plenty of chip designers. So why is the gap still there? The answer is not skill. It is a fixed cost. Designing a chip the normal way costs $2 million to $5 million before you sell a single unit. Most of that is not design work. It is: • physical layout work sent to an outside company: $1–2 million per chip • software licences for design tools: $0.5–1 million every year • a full set of photographic masks to print the chip: $0.5–1 million To pay that back you need volume. Millions of units, over several years, selling to a market that does not change its mind. Now look at what Indian defence and industry actually ask for. A power management chip for one avionics box might sell 10,000 units a year. It needs a specification nobody else uses. It must be screened to a military standard. You cannot build that chip against a $2–5 million setup cost. Not because it is hard. Because the sums do not work. So the big chip companies do the only sensible thing.

They offer a catalogue chip with the wrong specification, or an old chip that is about to be discontinued. The Indian buyer takes it, because there is nothing else. Nobody chose this. It is just what the costs force. And it has been this way for thirty years. 1.2 Then the law changed Something happened that a pure business analysis would miss. The Indian government stopped preferring Indian chips and started requiring them. Four rules now stack on top of each other: • DAP-2020 Buy (Indian-IDDM) puts Indian-designed products first. An Indian part beats an import before anyone compares prices. • Positive Indigenisation Lists (PILs) ban the import of named items after a stated date. The foreign supplier is not just at a disadvantage. It is removed from the bidding. • SRIJAN, a government portal, lists 37,696 imported items that defence companies want re- placed. The buyer publishes this list itself. • Make-II gives you a guaranteed order if your trials succeed. The buyer risks time. The supplier risks DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 8

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL development money. This combination is unusual, and it matters more than the market size. In a normal market, a cheap new competitor is answered with a price cut. Here, once an item is on a PIL, the foreign supplier cannot be chosen at any price. And once we are on an approved-vendor list, it becomes expensive for the customer to switch away from us. There is one catch in this argument. It is big enough that we will raise it ourselves. BUY(INDIAN) IS NOT THE SAME AS BUY(INDIAN-IDDM), AND FOR NOW WE ARE THE FIRST ONE The IDDM category depends on how much of the product’s value is Indian. It does not depend on where the design was done. Our first chips will be made in a factory in Wisconsin in the USA, and the radar chip in Germany. The design, the circuit code, the verification and the layout are all Indian. The silicon wafer is not. Read strictly, that probably puts us in Buy(Indian) and not Buy(Indian-IDDM), until we are making chips at SCL Mohali in India. Two things follow. First, Buy(Indian) still beats a straight import, and a PIL removes the import whichever category we are in. So the advantage is real. It is just one step lower than the strongest version of this argument. Second, this makes the SCL Mohali factory a business need, not a nice-tohave. That is why we keep it in the plan even though it is the least proven of our three factories. 1.3 Why now, and not five years ago Nothing above is new information. The import problem has been visible for thirty years. The engineering talent has been here for twenty. Four things changed recently, and all four had to change: Free chip design kits became real.

A factory design kit, or PDK, is the file set you need to design a chip for a specific factory. SkyWater released a free one called sky130 in 2020. A German institute, IHP, released one in 2023. Before that, “free PDK” meant a university process with no factory behind it. The free software tools improved too, to the point where they produce files a real factory will accept. RISC-V processors became good enough to ship. RISC-V is a free processor design standard. No licence fee, no royalty, no negotiation. Five years ago choosing it meant accepting a worse processor. The PIL deadlines are now. The dates in §11 fall between 2025 and 2028. A chip designed in 2021 would have been too early. One designed in 2029 will be too late. The smart-meter programme hit its peak years. Our largest commercial volume is a national meter programme, and its peak is in this decade. So the gap exists because of cost. And the law has now created a buyer who cannot fill that gap with imports. The rest of this document asks whether we can change the cost — and whether we have already shown that we can. DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL PART TWO We changed the cost, and we have real chips to prove it Our cost per finished chip is about ten times lower. Not because we are clever. Because four bills are not on our list. 2 Our costs, line by line Our claim is small and easy to test: Use an older factory process, a free design kit and an automated design flow. Together these cut the cost of a finished, tested, low-volume chip by about ten times. This makes a group of chips profitable that the big companies cannot profitably make. Indian law then keeps the customer with us for a decade. The important word is cannot. We are not saying we are cleverer than Texas Instruments. We are saying four bills on their list are not on ours. That changes which order sizes make money. Cost item Normal chip company Our way Physical layout $1–2 M sent outside, per chip done in-house on free kits — staff time only Design tool licences $0.5–1 M every year free tools — almost nothing Design time 12–18 months per chip design files in under 30 days; chips every 180 days Prototype masks $0.5–1 M for a full set shared factory run — ₹14.3 L on sky130, ₹34–80 L on IHP Testing and approval rolled into the project cost ₹40–80 L per chip, listed separately Total per chip $2–5 M ₹0.6–1.2 Cr including approval Three of those numbers are now quoted from the supplier’s own price page, and one of them shows we were wrong. A shared factory run on sky130 costs $14,950. That is ₹14.3 L at today’s rate. It returns 100 finished, packaged chips, and gives you about 15 mm² of space on the shared die. We had been saying ₹15–40 L per chip. So for nine of our ten chips we were charging ourselves too much. The tenth one goes the other way.

The radar chip uses the IHP factory, which charges by area: €5,110– 7,300 per mm². A radar front end of 6–10 mm² therefore costs ₹34–80 L. That is above the figure we claimed. IHP also runs a cheaper option at €2,800 per mm², but you must publish your design publicly under an open licence. A defence radar chip cannot do that, so it pays the full price. One price range for two different factories was wrong at both ends. Figure 6 now shows the real numbers. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 10

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL Every tool in the middle of Figure 2 is free software running on our own computers. Yosys for logic. OpenROAD for layout. TritonCTS for the clock network. TritonRoute for wiring. OpenRCX for extraction. Magic and KLayout for final checks. Four of the rows in the table above are an invoice for a normal chip company. For us they are staff time. So one more design attempt costs us almost nothing. That single fact is what lets a small company build a range of chips instead of one. 2.1 What this does and does not mean It does not mean we can beat a mass-market chip at ten million units. At that volume the big company has already paid off its setup cost, and it buys wafers cheaper than we do. We would lose. Saying otherwise would be the fastest way to lose your trust. What it means is this. A chip selling 10,000 units a year is a product for us. It is not a product for Texas Instruments. At ₹0.6–1.2 Cr total we can build it, get it approved, and sell it at 60–75 % gross margin. And in this market, the law stops the big company being chosen anyway. This is a low-end entry into a protected market. It is a known strategy with a known way of failing, and §12 deals with that failure directly instead of ignoring it. An argument about cost only matters if the method has actually made a chip. It has. 3 What we have already made Read this section differently from the rest. Nothing here is a forecast. A 130 nm test chip, made at SkyWater using our own automated flow. This is the key proof. It means our software produced a real design file, a real factory accepted it, and real working silicon came back. Our floating-point maths work at 130 nm is on that chip.

Every speed and cost claim in this document rests on it. DONE DONE A design on the TinyTapeout 6 shared chip. One of roughly 500 designs on a single 15 × 15 mm sky130 die. This is public and anyone can check it. One honest note: we should publish the exact project link, because right now we are asserting this rather than showing it. DONE ₹2.88 Cr of real revenue, before any chip exists. The Indian Army through MCEME: ₹1.01 Cr under contract, of which ₹23.01 L is delivered and ₹78.39 L is in progress. Infinis Agritech: ₹1.25 Cr for 50 kits, with a 40 % advance already received. Axitech Solar: ₹0.62 Cr for 25 kits. Normally a hardware company raises money, builds the product, then hopes it can sell. We are selling already. And this is board revenue, not chip revenue. All of it is hardware built around FPGAs. FPGAs are chips you can reprogram, useful for proving a design works before making a real chip. So what this money proves is that we can specify, build, sell and deliver a system to an Indian defence or industrial customer. That is not nothing. It is more than most companies have before their first chip. What it does not prove is that we can sell chips. A customer who buys a board is a different customer, at a different price, with a different approval process. Treating ₹2.88 Cr as proof of chip demand would be the easiest way to mislead you. So we are drawing the line ourselves. DONE DGS001, our DGFP4 demonstration board, is hardware we sell today. DESIGNED Circuit code tested on FPGAs. The lockstep microcontroller with fault testing, the motor control datapath, the meter measurement chain, the supervisor sensing chain, and the drone position engine. All exist as circuit code and run on an Artix-7 FPGA at 81.25 MHz. With dates. The IHP factory port.

SCL Mohali production. All six main prototypes sent for manufacture by March 2027. Commercial production from September 2027. PLANNED We would rather you find these on this page than in diligence. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 12

chunks.section: 3.1 One number people misread, and one that is genuinely open
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL Figure 3. Done, next, and still unproven, in three clearly different colours so nobody reading quickly can confuse them. 3.1 One number people misread, and one that is genuinely open 81.25 MHz is a limit of the FPGA, not of our design. It took eighteen builds to get the Artix-7 prototype working at that speed with the maths engines included. That proves the circuit code is correct and can be built. It says nothing about the real chip. The product is a 130 nm chip running at a fixed 200 MHz. We would rather explain this once, here, than have it read later as a performance claim. Which brings us to the one open item we would raise if we were reading this document. THE BIGGEST UNPROVEN CLAIM IN THIS DOCUMENT We say our chips run at 200 MHz. We have not yet published the timing analysis that proves it, and it is not clear which factory kit that analysis was run against. Running that analysis on sky130 and publishing the report is action 2 of seven in §14. It is the cheapest credibility we can buy. We are putting this here, in the evidence section, because that is where a reader would look for it. Cost and real silicon are the two halves of the claim. The next question an engineer asks is whether 130 nm is a real engineering choice or just the cheap option. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 13

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL PART THREE The machine: this process, this loop, this library 130 nm is the right process for these chips for reasons of physics, not price. The loop that turns that into a range of products runs every 198 days. And what builds up over time is not the chips. It is the library underneath them. 4 Why 130 nm is the right process, not the cheap one In chips, people assume newer is better. For this kind of chip that is simply wrong, and the reasons are physical. High voltage works here. 130 nm and 180 nm factory processes offer thick-oxide transistors and LDMOS devices. These handle 5 volts up to 120 volts directly. So a 28 V aircraft power rail, a 120 V motor supply and a 0.9 V digital core can all sit on one chip. On a newer, smaller process the power circuits move back onto the circuit board as separate parts. That is the opposite of what you want. More board space, more parts to buy, more things to fail. This is why four of our ten chips exist at all. Chip 1 has a 5–120 V converter next to a 200 MHz processor. Chip 3 puts an aircraft-standard input stage, an LDMOS power stage and four power rails on one chip. Chip 5 needs a 5 V-tolerant output ring. Chip 8 drives 0–12 V into a display panel across 3,840 outputs. None of these can be made on a newer process at any price. Radiation resistance comes from size. A cosmic ray can flip a stored bit. The bigger the transistor, the more charge is needed to flip it, so bigger transistors are harder to disturb. Protection methods such as DICE latches and triple redundancy cost chip area, and area is the one thing an older process has spare.

On chip 3 the power sequencer uses triple redundancy and DICE latches, and this costs a few percent of the chip. On a 28 nm process the same protection would eat into the part of the chip that justified using 28 nm. HOW FAR THIS CLAIM GOES We only claim design-level protection. We have no radiation dose figure, no latch-up test data and no radiation-hardened approval for these chips today. That dis- tinction matters in a defence conversation, so we state it rather than letting the phrase ”radiation tolerant” do vague work. Analogue circuits work better here, not worse. Analogue circuits handle continuous signals rather than ones and zeros. They need accurate resistors, good capacitors and transistors that match each other closely. Older processes have all three. Newer processes trade them away for density, and add leakage and mismatch that the analogue designer then spends area and power correcting. Chip 6 claims ±1 % accuracy from −40 °C to +125 °C. That comes DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 14

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL from a temperature-corrected reference circuit and closely matched resistors. For chip 5 the argu- ment reverses completely. A newer process is actively worse for a line driver. A line driver needs a 5 V-tolerant thick output ring with strong static-discharge protection. Newer processes do not have one. This is why interface chips from every major company are still made on older processes today. One place the process is a hard limit. Chip 7 is a 4D radar front end. It cannot be built on ordinary CMOS. The sky130 process will not reach 77 GHz. Not slowly, not expensively. Not at all. The IHP SG13G2 process is a 130 nm SiGe process with special high-speed transistors that reach about 350 GHz. This is the transistor type that real 77 GHz car radar uses. So the design splits into two chips, one on each process, with the boundary at the analogue-to-digital converter. One result of this belongs here and not in a footnote. You cannot prototype a 77 GHz front end on an FPGA. FPGA testing covers the digital half only. The high-frequency half is proven in silicon or not at all. AND ONE PLACE WHERE A FREE DESIGN KIT IS A PROBLEM, NOT A BENEFIT Everything above is true of the factory process. It is not yet true of the parts library. A paid 130 nm design kit comes with a tested library of analogue building blocks: reference circuits, protection cells rated to a stated level, memory. A free kit does not. So the ±15 kV protection ring on chip 5, the temperature-stable reference on chip 3 and the memory on chip 1 are targets with no tested example to copy. We have to build and prove each one in silicon before it becomes a datasheet number. That is real work and real schedule.

It is a bigger technical risk than the 200 MHz question, and §14 carries it as its own line rather than hiding it inside ”design”. 4.1 And what this process cannot do The limits belong in the same section as the advantages. A reader who finds them later will assume we hid them. At 130 nm and 200 MHz we cannot build a high-performance AI accelerator, object recognition at video speed, a central car computer with multi-gigahertz processors and fast memory, or drone swarm control. Those all need much smaller processes. A 28 nm process gets you some of them. None of them can be claimed at 130 nm at any clock speed. That is exactly why the D100 drone chip is on a separate track using a 28 nm process and separate money. It is also why chip 9 says on its own face that it handles the local layer of a car’s electronics and not the central computer. The strategy draft states ”10 new SKUs every year” and ”over 1,000 active SKUs by Year 5”. Those are inconsistent by 20x: 10/yr x 5 yr = 50. 50 SKUs on mature nodes is already an aggressive catalogue for a company this size. 1,000 would need 200 tapeouts a year. Pick one number before this goes to an investor. Shown below: the 50-SKU ramp, which is what ”10 per year” actually produces. The panel also corrects an arithmetic mistake in an earlier internal draft, because that draft’s ”1,000 chips” and ”10 per year” could not both be true. The process is right and the cost is right. What turns those two facts into a range of products, rather than one product, is the loop. 5 One loop every 198 days Progress here is not measured in milestones. It is measured in factory runs. Our hiring plan, our cash need and how fast the product range grows all follow from how long one run takes, and from which half of it can be repeated. chunks.section: Design: 30 days or less. Specification, then circuit code, then verification, then layout, then final
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL Design: 30 days or less. Specification, then circuit code, then verification, then layout, then final checks. Verification and circuit code go back and forth with each other. Nothing else in the chain does. This half is limited by how many engineers we have, and engineers are what money buys. The manufacturing gate. To go ahead you need enough verification coverage, no timing failures, and a clean layout check. These are targets today, not history, and the figures say so. Silicon: 168 days. Masks, wafers, packaging, testing. This half cannot be repeated at all. One mistake costs a whole cycle. That is why we enforce the design-complete gate before the factory window, not during it. That 168 is not our estimate. It is the gap between sending the design and receiving packaged chips on the published factory calendar. From 16 September 2026 to 3 March 2027 on the CI2609 run. From 7 December 2026 to 25 May 2027 on CI2612. We had been saying “about 150 days”, which was a rounded guess. So one full cycle is 30 + 168 = 198 days, not 180. We would rather correct our own headline than have you find the factory’s calendar and correct it for us. We keep the name because the design half is the part we control. The arithmetic is in Figure 6. 5.1 There are two speeds here, not one The 30-day figure is for digital chips. It would be misleading to let it stand for the whole range. A digital block on an automated flow really does finish in weeks. An analogue block does not, because you cannot check a reference circuit or a protection ring on a computer. You need silicon in your hand.

chunks.section: 5.2 Who actually makes the production batch
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 5.2 Who actually makes the production batch The right-hand side of Figure 6 only works if somebody will make a dedicated mask set and a full batch of wafers. That needs stating carefully rather than assuming. The published position is prototypes only. Our factory service’s own FAQ says the programme is “focused on prototype volumes (100 units per design)”, with production volumes planned “based on market demand”. Read literally, that means the production masks and first wafer batches that ₹2.26 Cr of this round is meant to buy had no named supplier at all. That would be a bigger hole than the packaging gap in §10. In conversation they have said they are willing to support a direct production route. That is a real change and it is why this is no longer just a hope. It is also not a contract, a price quote or a schedule, and we will not present it as one. The next thing to get is a written price quote for a production mask set and a first wafer batch. That is action 3 of seven in §14. One result of this is uncomfortable and belongs here. If the same supplier handles both the prototype and the production route, then our dependence on one supplier gets worse, not better. It now covers the whole path from design to volume. The backup is unglamorous but real. The sky130 process is SkyWater’s own production process, so a direct factory relationship is possible. And SCL Mohali is the Indian backup. 5.3 The boundary we would rather state than be caught on 180 days ends with silicon in your hand, not with a product you can sell. Commercial chips ship 6– 9 months after that: characterisation, datasheet, test program development, approval batches, customer design work.

chunks.section: 5.2 Who actually makes the production batch
chunks.text: A screened defence chip adds another 9–12 months of MIL-883, JSS and CEMILAC checks, and that clock is not ours to speed up at any price. We say this because the alternative is a schedule that slips in front of you later. We budget ₹40–80 L per chip for approval as a separate line rather than hiding it in overheads, and §10 explains what that money actually buys. A 198-day loop gives us one chip per cycle. It does not explain how a small team builds fifty chips. That comes from what builds up between the loops. 6 How a product range builds up: blocks, not chips We are one of about 500 designs on a single TinyTapeout die. That is a real credential and it points at a real strategy. But the strategy only survives a chip investor’s questions if we change one word first, and we would rather change it ourselves.
