chunks.section: 6.1 What a shared die can and cannot do
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 6.1 What a shared die can and cannot do TinyTapeout puts hundreds of small designs on one die behind a shared wrapper. Each design gets a fixed tile of space, and a switch picks which one connects to the shared pins. Only one design works at a time. That is excellent for what it does, and completely unable to do four things: • Space. A tile is about 0.02 mm². That is a few hundred to a few thousand logic gates. A motor controller with a power converter, a 16-bit converter, seven output channels and a processor is several mm². No sellable chip fits in a tile. • Analogue and high voltage. The wrapper is digital only. No high-voltage devices, no reference circuits, no converters, no thick output ring, no high-speed radar transistors. Chips 3, 5, 6, 7 and the output stage of chip 8 cannot be tested this way at all. • Using many pins at once. The pins are shared and time-switched. You cannot test 3,840 display out- puts, or seven motor channels, or four radar receivers. You can show a digital block works. You cannot measure noise, power supply rejection, or accuracy across temperature from a tile. • Datasheet measurements. 6.2 The change of word The mistake is calling a tile a chip. It is not. It is a building block. And every chip in our range breaks down into digital building blocks, and those do fit in a tile: the motor control datapath, the tuning loop, the meter filter, the fault table, the noise filters, the lockstep comparator, the display timing generator, the network shaper, the encryption cores, the memory controller, the radar processing control.

chunks.section: 6.1 What a shared die can and cannot do
chunks.text: Do not say “1,000 chips in five years.” A chip means a datasheet, an approval, a test program and a place on an approved-vendor list. A thousand of those cannot be built. A chip investor will reject it immediately, and that then makes every other number in the document look careless. Say “1,000 silicon-tested building blocks, combining into about 50 approved chips, 10–20 of them in vol- ume.” Same ambition. Completely believable. And it explains how the chips get built quickly, which the other version does not. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 21
DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 22

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL Level Vehicle Unit Cost each What it proves 5-yr count shared die, TinyTapeout type digital block $100–500 the block works in silicon 1,000 shared factory run full chip ₹14.3 L sky130 · ₹34–80 L IHP the chip meets its spec 50 dedicated mask set production chip ₹1 Cr+ we can ship it in volume 10–20 The three levels are a thousand times apart in cost, and that is the point. You spend a few hundred dollars to learn what would otherwise cost ₹1 Cr to learn. There are two entry routes, not one. Digital blocks enter at level 1. Analogue and high-voltage blocks cannot, and must enter at level 2 as their own test chips with their own pins and power supplies. Any plan that puts the power management chip or the radar front end on a shared tile is wrong. Saying so protects everything else here. 6.3 The precedent every informed reader will think of A free design kit, a shared die and a range of small chips is not a new idea. The closest attempt ran at large scale. The shared-run programme that made sky130 available produced several hundred manufactured designs over four years with major corporate funding. It did not produce a commercial range of approved chips. Anyone who knows this field will think of it within thirty seconds of reading this section. So we would rather say what we think is different than pretend it did not happen. Three differences. Weigh each one yourself: • Those runs were nearly all level 1 in our own scheme. Blocks and demonstrations on a shared wrap- per, which is what a shared wrapper is good for. Almost none went on to a full chip run, and essentially none went to a dedicated mask set.

That programme proved blocks and then stopped, because proving blocks was its purpose. Levels 2 and 3 are the part nobody has demonstrated on a free design kit, including us, and §14 says so. • They had no protected demand. A hobby or research chip has no approved-vendor list waiting for it and no import ban creating a buyer. The legal position in §1 is what turns the same technical approach into a business, and it did not exist for them. • We are not selling the factory run. We are selling the chip. A run service earns money from the number of designs. We earn money from approved chips, which is a much harder target and a much smaller number. Fifty, not a thousand. If those three do not convince you, then the honest answer is that this is the weakest part of the plan on past evidence. That is exactly why §14 says the round has to prove levels 2 and 3, not level 1. 6.4 Why this is a real advantage and not just a cost trick A block proven once in silicon can be reused in every chip that needs it. After five years the asset is not the number of tiles. It is a library of silicon-tested blocks that a competitor cannot copy without spending the same five years. The lockstep comparator tested for chip 4 is the same block that makes chip 9’s safety section and the drone chip’s backup system believable. That is how this compounds, and it is why the range can grow by several chips a year without several times the staff. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 23

chunks.section: 6.5 Two things we would argue with in our own plan
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 6.5 Two things we would argue with in our own plan Custom chip-to-chip connections stop us selling a single die. We chose not to use the UCIe industry standard. That avoids a real area and power cost, but it means no other company can buy one of our dies as a component. If selling dies is ever the plan, the connection standard has to be chosen now. Changing it later is a redesign. Packaging is a supply chain that is not yet in our plan. The end goal is six chips in one package: power, motor drive, communications, safety, control and analogue, with the 28 nm AI chip joining later. This multiplies volume, because one packaged product contains six chips. But it needs an assembly partner, package-level testing, and an answer to what happens when one chip in six is faulty. That last question forces you to test every chip before assembly, and §10 carries it as a cost and a schedule line rather than a detail. One method, one library. The next question is which factories it runs in, and whether ”works on any process” survives contact with an analogue circuit. 7 One method, three factories One design method, three factories, built to move between processes. The three are not alterna- tives. They are a sequence with three different jobs.

chunks.section: 8.1 Every missing feature is a decision
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 8.1 Every missing feature is a decision A reviewer will read the second half of that table as a list of gaps unless we explain each one. No caches. A cache is a small fast memory that keeps recently used data. It usually helps, but sometimes it misses and then the access takes far longer. These are control chips that must respond in a guaranteed time. A cache turns a guaranteed worst case into an average, and that is the wrong trade for a motor loop, a power sequencer or a safety monitor. Our processor goes straight to closely attached memory with a fixed access time. Chip 1’s hardware control loop responds in under 1 microsecond, and that number only means something because nothing in the path can miss. No branch prediction. Same reason, plus chip area. A cost you always pay is easier to plan for than one you usually avoid. And these control loops are short and dominated by data processing rather than branching. No floating-point unit. Every calculation in our range uses fixed-point maths by design. Fixed-point is smaller, faster, and gives exactly the same answer on every chip. That matters when the same calculation must match between a screened chip and a commercial one. Our floating-point work at 130 nm sits on the test chip as a separate engine, not inside the control processor. No compressed instructions. Compressed instructions save memory space. That matters when instruction memory is off the chip and expensive. Here it is on the chip and sized to the job, and removing the feature removes an alignment case from the fetch path. Memory protection instead of a full memory manager. These chips run bare-metal code or a small realtime operating system.

chunks.section: 8.1 Every missing feature is a decision
chunks.text: What they need is to keep the secure start-up code, the application and the safety monitor separate from each other. Memory protection regions do exactly that, at a fraction of the chip area a full memory manager needs. 8.2 Why 200 MHz is enough, and what the number is not Because the processor is a controller, not a calculator. In every chip the heavy work is done by dedicated hardware: the motor control pipeline, the meter filter chain, the display pixel pipeline, the radar processing. The processor sets that hardware up, watches it, handles faults and talks to the host system. The clock speed that matters is the dedicated hardware’s, and that hardware is sized by how many parallel lanes it has, not by megahertz. Which means 200 MHz is a target for the processor, not a promise for every chip, and we have been using the number too loosely. Three points go with it. It applies to the DGridRiscV processor and the bus around it. Several chips do not need it at all: chip 6 is a comparator with a watchdog, and chip 5 is a line driver whose limit is signal timing, not clock speed. And the chips that do want it will each reach their own speed, because a 3,840-output display driver and a six-channel meter front end are not the same timing problem. What we will publish is a measured speed for each chip once the analysis is run, not one number for all nine. That is the machine: the process, the loop, the library, the factories and the processor. What follows is what we build with it. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 28

Getting from working silicon to some- thing a customer can buy is a separate problem, and it is where hardware plans usually break. 9 Ten chips, and what each one is for Chip Product Process Why it exists BLDC motor controller 130 nm two-chip driver-plus-processor sets combined into one Smart-meter chip 130 nm 250 M meter rollout; tamper detection is required in tenders High-reliability power chip sky130 →SCL 180 nm 28 V power rails in every avionics box Lockstep microcontroller 130 nm the fault-tested processor, made into a product Interface transceiver 130 nm replaces discontinued parts; highest attach volume Voltage supervisor sky130 →SCL simplest chip — goes through approval first 4D radar front end IHP SiGe + CMOS the one chip with a hard physical process limit Display driver 130 nm high voltage named on PIL-5, BEL, due Dec 2027 Car zonal controller 130 nm local layer only — the central computer is out of scope Track B D100 drone chip TSMC 28 nm the high-performance one; separate round, revenue-gated Two ordering decisions are deliberate, not accidental. Commercial chips go first. The motor controller and the meter chip sell fastest and build credibility. The defence versions follow behind them on the same approved silicon, at prices 10 to 100 times higher. And the simplest chip goes through approval first. Chip 6 is a supervisor with one comparator chain and a short test list, so it carries the MIL-883 screening process for everything behind it.

If that process holds a surprise, we would rather find it on a supervisor than on a four-rail power chip. The ten architecture drawings that follow each show the internal blocks, the timing behaviour, example performance curves, a market panel with volumes and prices, and where FPGA testing stops and the real chip begins. The circuit code already exists and has been fault-tested, carried over from the drone chip programme. Status. FPGA testing at 81.25 MHz, then a 130 nm chip at 200 MHz. A line driver needs a 5 V-tolerant thick output ring, and newer processes do not have one. Where it sells, and how many. It is the simplest chip we build, so it carries the MIL-883 screening process for everything behind it. §10 explains that decision. Status. Imported zonal controllers and gateway chips that bridge older car networks to Ethernet. Why this process. A gateway is about how many channels it has and how predictable its timing is. The Indian drone market was worth $1.2 to $1.3 billion in 2025, and is forecast at $2.7 to $3.2 billion by 2030–34. Flight control with position tracking sells at $100 to $300. chunks.section: 10.1 What ₹40–80 L per chip actually buys
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 10.1 What ₹40–80 L per chip actually buys Approval is not one test. For a commercial industrial chip it is a defined sequence with a defined number of samples. For a screened defence chip it is longer. Characterisation means measuring the chip across manufacturing variation, voltage and temperature, on enough units to write a datasheet with real limits instead of simulated ones. Reliability means hightemperature life testing, temperature cycling, humidity, static-discharge and latch-up testing. And for defence versions, screening means burn-in, electrical testing at temperature extremes, leak testing on the package seal, and the paperwork trail that MIL-883, JSS and CEMILAC approval require. The reliability and screening steps take calendar time. More money does not make them shorter. Five of the eight steps to a screened chip are in that category. This is why the plan sends commercial chips first, and pushes chip 6 through the process early — specifically to learn where it slows down before four other chips are queued behind it. One factory run cannot approve a chip, and that costs money. A shared run gives you one set of wafers, usually made at typical settings. An approval needs material from more than one batch, so that batch-tobatch variation is included in the samples. A defence screening process will ask for it. So ₹40–80 L per chip is honestly a commercial-grade approval figure. A screened version needs extra material, and for the analogue chips that means extra factory runs, not just extra test time. We have sized the round for four approvals rather than seven for exactly this reason, and §13 names the three that are not funded.

chunks.section: 10.1 What ₹40–80 L per chip actually buys
chunks.text: 10.2 The cost line that was missing from our own model TESTING WILL BECOME THE BOTTLENECK BEFORE DESIGN DOES A test program, a test circuit board and machine time are not covered by the approval budget. And for a package holding several chips, the test time multiplies rather than adds. In our earlier plans this line did not appear at all. A ₹1.2 Cr testing line is now listed separately in the use of funds. The assembly partner and the package-test company still need to be named, and that is the largest remaining gap in this document. We would rather you read it here than find it. There is a second consequence for the multi-chip package. If one chip in six is faulty, the whole package is scrap unless every chip was tested before assembly. So you must test every chip individually first. That is both a cost line and a schedule line, and neither existed in our model before this document. 10.3 The customer approves the supplier, not just the chip This is the gap that an aggressive read of our own document found, and it is the one we had thought about least. Being on an approved-vendor list is not granted to a chip. It is granted to a company. And a defence or car customer audits the company before it audits the chip. They want a quality management system such as ISO 9001, or AS9100 for aerospace. They want records of approved suppliers. They want static-discharge controls. They want to trace every unit back to its wafer. They want a documented process for notifying customers of changes. And they want a second source, or a policy for last-time purchases. None of that is diﬀicult, and none of it is expensive next to a mask set. But it takes calendar time, it needs somebody whose job it is, and it does not currently appear anywhere in our use of funds.

chunks.section: 10.1 What ₹40–80 L per chip actually buys
chunks.text: A company with excellent silicon and no quality system does not get onto an approved list. The sales process in §11 has an approval step that quietly assumes this problem is solved. It is not. We would rather name it here than discover it in a customer audit. It is now in the risk table in §14. An approved chip is still not revenue. It becomes revenue through two completely different sales processes, both using the same chip. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 52

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL PART FIVE Two ways to sell the same chip, and why nobody can copy us The commercial route is self-service. The defence route is relationship-led and protected by law. One ap- proved chip, two prices 10 to 100 times apart. And a big competitor with no available answer. 11 Two ways to sell the same chip Selling chips is not a pitch. It is a sequence of things you hand the customer. A design engineer downloads a datasheet, decides in ten minutes whether the chip can work, buys an evaluation board with a credit card, gets it running in a week, and only then does anyone discuss commercial terms. If any item in that chain is missing, the process stops there, no matter how good the silicon is. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 53
DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 54

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL That is why ₹1.0 Cr of the round is sales and working capital. And it is why the distributor conversation matters more than it looks. A catalogue chip that is not in stock and cannot be found in a search does not exist to the engineer who needs it. The defence route works differently. You find the item on SRIJAN or a PIL. You have a technical discussion with the defence company. You supply trial units. You get a Make-II or direct order. Then you go on the approved-vendor list. The trial stage is where a small company wins, because the buyer is risking time rather than money, and an Indian-designed part beats an import before price is discussed. Both routes use the same approved chip, at prices 10 to 100 times apart. That is the real eﬀiciency of having a range, and it is why low volume is still good business here. 11.1 What we found when we read the government lists ourselves We read the defence ministry’s 5th PIL — 346 items, scanned, so we had to run text recognition on it — and DMA lists 1, 2, 3 and 5, directly rather than relying on summaries. What we found was not what we expected, and it changed how we sell. The lists name boxes, not chips. They list swappable units, assemblies and spare parts. Most of PIL-5 is bushes, valves, pumps, gaskets and optical filters. There is no chip-level item anywhere in what we read. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 55
DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 56

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL So our entry point is one level down: supplying the silicon inside a listed box. That is a real route. It is how every chip supplier into defence actually works. But it is a completely different first meeting from “here is an item on your list, we will build it”. Pretending otherwise wastes a defence company’s time and our credibility. Electronics items we confirmed, that match our range: List Item Owner / platform Due Matches PIL-5 BLDC motor with encoder anti-tank missile Dec 2025 chip 1 PIL-5 DC-DC converter, 4 A, 16–40 V in BEL · tank Dec 2026 chip 3 PIL-5 DC-DC converter 12 V BEL · tank Dec 2028 chip 3 PIL-5 Isolation amplifier BEL · tank Dec 2028 nearby PIL-5 Digital receiver (SDC V2) BEL · electronic warfare Dec 2026 chip 7 family PIL-5 Synthesizer BEL · electronic warfare Dec 2026 chip 7 family PIL-5 17-inch rugged display BEL · Defence Electronics Dec 2027 chip 8 PIL-5 Radio altimeter HAL · Dornier Dec 2025 chip 7 variant PIL-5 Magnetometer HAL · LCH Dec 2025 nearby DMA Radar warning receiver Su-30 MKI, Mi-17 Dec 2025 chip 7 family DMA Weapon locating / battlefield radar Army 2022–26 chip 7 family DMA Power amplifiers, 10 W and 2–4 kW Air Force Dec 2021 IHP SiGe DMA Software defined radio, manpack all services Dec 2022 future DMA IRNSS receiver; GNSS jammer; GNSS spoofing Navy / Air Force Dec 2022 future DMA Proximity fuze, 76/62 SRGM Navy — future The highest-value match is also the least specified. The BEL electronic-warfare digital receiver and synthesizer are the best matches in the whole list. And the one-line entries give neither the frequency band nor the dynamic range. That single answer decides whether we use the SiGe process or ordinary CMOS.

Which then decides the cost, the schedule, and whether it is one chip or two. It needs a conversation with BEL, not more desk research. It is action 4 of seven in §14. Two routes, one chip, and a set of laws that removes the competitor from one of them. The obvious question is what that competitor does about it. 11.2 The rule that guards the money: no buyer, no build A chip gets build money only when its buyer has a name — our own product needs it, a government make-in-India list names it, a defence filing names it, a tender asks for it, or a customer signs a letter. Nothing else counts. Not enthusiasm, not a market report, not a deadline. Today the scoreboard reads: eleven chips have a named buyer and may spend — 1 (anchor: Airgap Technology), 3, 4 (anchor: MCEME, contracted), 5, 6, 7, 8 (buyer and date on a gov- ernment list: BEL, Dec 2027), 10 (anchor: Chakravayu CPDL), plus the security chip and the drone-navigation helper our own products need. Four wait on one signature — chip 2 (Rip- ple’s letter; our biggest revenue line, gated first on purpose so the rule is seen to be real), chip 9 (a vehicle maker’s pilot), the cockpit display controller (rides chip 8’s buyer), and the avion- ics power part (opens when chip 3 passes screening). Eight are on hold until a programme, mandate or letter names them — and spend nothing meanwhile. The newest two are the V2X vehicle-communications set (SKUs 21–22): a 5.9 GHz radio front-end on IHP’s radio-grade 130 nm process, and an LTE-class road-safety modem on the same fab’s digital side, carrying the message- signing security engine built from chip 15’s block and leaning on chips 4 or 9 as host. The bound is stated: the newer 5G flavour of the standard is a finer-node problem, and we do not claim it.

India has no V2X mandate yet, so both wait — a chip on hold is the rule working, not a gap. Three kinds of buyers run on three clocks, and mixing them up is how forecasts lie: • A list entry — permission, not an order. The import ban arrives on the list’s date; orders trickle in over 2–4 years. Good for the future; never counted in this year’s number. • A defence filing — the real order path. File, build a sample at our cost, pass trials — about 15–18 months — and then the order is assured by rule. The only path we count revenue on. • A tender win — the fast clock. Get written into a tender’s requirements and ship on its schedule. Meters and fans live here. Hidden step: just registering as a vendor takes 6–12 months — it is on our timeline now. DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 11.3 Who actually buys — names, numbers, dates (September 2026) Facts as of September 2026, sources on file. Labelled so nobody mistakes the size of a door for an order of ours. • Smart meters. 20.33 crore meters sanctioned nationally; 7.24 crore installed by June 2026; tenders for ∼5 crore meters running now in Haryana, MP, Punjab and Tamil Nadu; the scheme runs to March 2028. The two biggest doors: Genus (order book ₹24,020 crore; an 18-million- meter yearly factory) and Adani Energy (over 4.7 crore meters in hand). Their orders, not ours — this shows the size of the door. Our anchor, Ripple Metering, is the named first door. • Defence. A sixth import-ban list arrived in August 2026: 405 items, about ₹3,070 crore of business. Over 33,000 items sit on the SRIJAN portal for indigenisation, and defence companies have already placed ₹7,572 crore of orders on Indian vendors. BEL runs the display line our chip 8 answers. • Drones. The Army now physically tears drones apart to verify where every part comes from; recent orders (₹137 crore, then ₹105 crore, to ideaForge) went only to platforms that passed. An Indian-made drone brain is exactly what that inspector wants to find. ₹40,000 crore sits in the new emergency-procurement cycle. Our anchor here: Chakravayu CPDL. • Electric vehicles. 14 lakh electric two-wheelers sold in FY26, up 22%, crossing 2 lakh in July 2026 alone. Five controller makers to design into: TVS, Bajaj, Ather, Hero Vida, Ola. Our anchor, Airgap Technology, builds the motors these controllers drive. 12 Why a big competitor cannot copy this DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 58

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL In the commercial market we are against Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, Renesas, Microchip and ST. They win on range, distribution, software tools and trust. We do not claim otherwise. What we do is serve a shape of demand their costs exclude: a 10,000-unit programme with a specific requirement and a screening step. In the defence market the competitor is not a chip company winning on merit. It is an import that the law is progressively removing from the bidding. Our real competitor there is another Indian company, and what separates us is who has finished silicon and a screening process first. Today, we do. In the drone market it is Qualcomm’s QRB5165 and nothing else integrated. That is a Track B argument, funded separately. A big competitor has three possible answers, and all three are blocked. Cut the price does not help, because the barrier is paying off the setup cost on a small programme, not the unit price. And after a PIL date the price is irrelevant, because the chip cannot be chosen at all. Open a low-cost design centre in India is real, and several have. It reduces their engineering cost but not their $2–5 million per-chip layout and mask cost. And it does not make the chip Indian-designed for DAP-2020 purposes. Buy the new company is the likely ending, and it is an acceptable outcome for this round. But it is not a plan we depend on. 12.1 How this strategy fails, said plainly Companies that enter at the low end often get stuck there. The pattern is well documented. The new company becomes dependent on its protected corner, never builds the ability to compete on merit, and gets squeezed when the protection ends.

It would be dishonest to present the entry without the failure mode. Our answer is the block library and the process roadmap. What compounds is not the protected socket. It is the library of silicon-tested blocks, and the method that produced it. Both can move to processes and markets where nobody is protecting us. The move to 90, 55 and 45 nm from 2028 exists for exactly this reason, and it is driven by channel count and signal processing throughput, not by clock speed. That is the whole argument. What is left is the money: what it buys, what it proves, and what could stop it. 12.2 What if Chinese prices crash — and our stop rules The cure for loving your own forecast is a second forecast where things go badly. Here is FY31 re-priced as if Chinese chips flood India — and note which row the crash cannot touch: Row Our plan (₹Cr) If prices crash Why Smart meters 480 ∼340 tenders squeeze prices: −30% Motor controllers 220 ∼130 the most exposed chip: −40% Defence (screened) 200 200 import-banned market — the crash cannot reach it Drone brain 65 ∼55 Army origin checks blunt the war Vehicle gateway 35 ∼25 open market: −30% Total 1,000 ∼750 even then the plan survives, and the next round still triggers And our stop rules — written now, with dates, so nobody bends them later in an excited meeting: • S1. If Ripple (or another meter maker) has not signed by the day chip 2’s factory order is due, that chip waits one full cycle and its money moves to chips 1 and 3. No exceptions, however the meeting feels. • S2. If chip 6 fails military screening twice, every document moves defence revenue out by twelve months, within thirty days. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 60

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL • S3. In FY29 we check Chinese prices properly — duties and tender rules included. If they land below what the chip costs us to make, we leave the fan market and keep e-scooters plus our own products. The walk-away price gets calculated this quarter, calmly. • S4. If the government factory in Mohali runs more than two cycles late, we say so publicly and lean on our two other factories. No quiet slipping of dates. One piece of homework we owe ourselves this quarter: find out, properly, what Chinese chips will really cost in India in FY29 — duties and tender rules included — before an investor asks us. And one line for §12.1’s list: the meter row fails loudest — if no letter is signed by the factory-order date, that ₹480 crore moves out a year, and the plan still closes near ₹520 crore on the other rows. 13 What ₹10 Cr buys, and what it proves Under contract today: ₹1.01 Cr. DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL The FY31 figure is coverage of categories, not market share. By year 5 our range covers most of the olderprocess chip categories India imports. It only works because the meter and motor volume uses the same approved chips the defence versions use. One approval, two prices, two markets. We then ran the obvious check on our own number, and it did not fully pass. WE CHECKED OUR OWN FY31 SPLIT, AND PART OF IT DOES NOT HOLD Take the FY31 figure, divide it between the nine chips, then divide each chip’s share by its price. That gives the number of units each line needs, and therefore what share of the market it needs. At ₹95.39 per dollar, the meter chip needs 72 % of our stated volume band and the motor chip 42 %, at mid prices. At the top of both bands those fall to 34 % and 19 %. If we cap every chip at a 30 % share, the nine chips can still carry ₹1,324 Cr. So the total holds and the split does not — 70 % of FY31 sits on two chips, while chips 9, 7 and 4 are planned at under a tenth of theirs. We would rebalance before an institutional round. One caution on how to read those percentages. They treat our stated volume band as the whole market. An investor’s own sizing model reads the same bands as our target inside a larger category, and quotes separate category sizes for five of the ten chips. On that reading the shares are 11–30 % of the category, not 42–72 % of the market. That is probably the better reading, and it would remove the alarming figures above. We have not yet rebuilt the table that way because a category size exists for only five chips. What survives either reading is the concentration, which is why the rebalancing point stands.

13.1 What the money physically produces The first question a hardware investor asks is not about milestones. It is about units. So: Prototypes 600 chips six factory runs × 100 packaged parts. Not sellable — not approved, and 0.6 % of one year’s need Production 94,000–165,000 production mask sets and first wafer batches for chips 1 and 2 only Value of those batches ₹2–9 Cr at the $3–8 and $2–5 prices already stated FY27 needs 100,000 units at an average $4.50 — the two first batches cover FY27 completely FY28 needs 707,000 units about eleven more batches per chip, which are working capital against orders, not setup cost, and not in this round The arithmetic: a 200 mm wafer, 3 mm unusable at the edge, 90 % of the rest usable after cutting lanes, 85 % of chips working, 25 wafers per batch. The chip sizes are engineering estimates — 8 to 15 mm² for chip 1 with its high-voltage section, 6 to 10 mm² for chip 2. That is the sensitive input. If chip 1 comes out at 15 mm² rather than 8, the answer drops to the bottom of the range and FY27 coverage gets tight. We will publish measured sizes with the first layout. This is the whole case for funding a production batch inside a seed round. A prototype chip costs about ₹14,300. A production chip costs ₹120 to ₹260 in mask cost spread across the batch. There is no volume at which buying more prototype runs beats buying one mask set. The prototype run proves the chip. Only the mask set can sell it. A round that funded prototypes and stopped would produce 600 chips, no revenue, and a company that must raise again before it can invoice anyone. chunks.section: 13.2 The tightest link, now that we have the factory dates
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 13.2 The tightest link, now that we have the factory dates Six designs split across the CI2609 and CI2612 runs do get sent for manufacture before March 2027, so that milestone holds. But chips arrive on 3 March 2027 for the first three and 25 May 2027 for the second three. That leaves roughly four months to characterise, release and reach production by September 2027. That is the tightest link in this plan. The fix is a sequencing decision, not money: put chips 1 and 2 — the two the revenue plan depends on — on the CI2609 run, and let the later run carry the chips whose revenue is FY29 and beyond. 13.3 Money, time and the size of the team An investor’s second question, after whether the technology is real, is how long the money lasts and how many people are spending it. This document did not answer either until we were asked. So: Runway on ₹10 Cr 24 months, to the March 2027 milestone and into first production Average monthly spend about ₹41 L, weighted early to engineering and late to masks and approval Engineers funded 5–7 people on ₹2.4 Cr over 24 months — ₹1.2 Cr a year at Hyderabad costs What that team is 1 senior, 3 mid-level, 2 junior, of whom 2 are analogue designers Founder pay partly deferred, which is what makes 5–7 fit inside ₹1.2 Cr a year Revenue during the period ₹4 Cr in FY27 and ₹28 Cr in FY28, of which ₹2.88 Cr is already live And the honest problem in those numbers. Five to seven engineers, only two of them analogue, against four analogue-heavy chips each needing two or three silicon attempts, is thin. We ran that check ourselves at ₹1.2 Cr a year of fully loaded cost and it does not support a bigger team.

That is the real reason the round funds four approvals and not seven, and why chips 5, 7 and 8 are scheduled into the second cycle and later, rather than promised in this window. 13.4 The ask ₹10 Cr angel or seed, on a simple convertible instrument, capped below the institutional round. It funds six parallel factory runs, four approvals, and working capital. That means seven older- process chips from architecture through tested silicon and into approval, including production mask sets and first wafer batches for chips 1 and 2. Which leaves the only honest way to end a document like this: what could stop it, and what we would fix first. 13.5 What each chip must earn — the one table Our funnel ends at ₹1,000 crore by FY31 and calls it an ambitious plan. chunks.section: 14.1 The seven things we would fix first, in order of value
chunks.text: DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 14.1 The seven things we would fix first, in order of value 1. Publish what the 130 nm test chip actually cost, and what was on it. This is the correction we least wanted and most needed. The whole cost argument in §2 rests on a ₹0.6–1.2 Cr figure that has never been done once. Except that we have already made a chip on this method, so a real number exists and we are simply not showing it. It either supports the claim or it does not, and either way a reader is entitled to it before being asked to trust the estimate. It also answers the question behind it: did that chip contain any analogue? 2. Run the timing analysis on sky130 and publish it, per chip. The 200 MHz number is the biggest claim we make and it is currently a design target. One report per chip turns it into a fact, and it is the cheapest credibility available to us. 3. Get the production price quote in writing. Our factory service has said it is willing to support a direct production route. Their published FAQ still says prototypes only. A quoted mask set and first wafer batch turns the whole production half of this plan from a verbal indication into a number. That is the difference between a company that can invoice in FY27 and one that cannot. 4. Get the BEL electronic-warfare specification. It unlocks the highest-value matches on the government lists, and settles the SiGe-versus-CMOS question that gates the whole chip 7 family. 5. Replace target numbers with measured numbers. When the first 130 nm batch comes back, swap in real coverage, timing, yield and test results for the current targets. Every drawing in this document is built to accept that swap without being redrawn.

chunks.section: 14.1 The seven things we would fix first, in order of value
chunks.text: That one change turns a plan into a track record. 6. Name the packaging and testing partners. It is the largest unaddressed gap in the model, and the easiest one for a technical reviewer to find. 7. Publish the TinyTapeout 6 project link. A public shared-die manufacture that anyone can verify is cheap credibility, and right now we are asserting it rather than showing it. None of the seven needs this round to happen, and five of them we can do in the next sixty days. We list them because a document that only argues its strengths is not a document you can act on. And because the first two came out of arguing against ourselves, not out of a reviewer’s comments. WHAT WE ARE ACTUALLY ASKING YOU TO BELIEVE Not that we can out-engineer Texas Instruments. We cannot, and this document does not claim to. Not that the FY31 number is a forecast. It is a scenario, and we have just shown you which part of it does not hold. What we are asking you to believe is smaller and easier to check than either. That an older process, a free design kit and an automated method take about ten times out of the cost of a finished lowvolume chip. That we have already made silicon using that method. That Indian law has created a buyer who cannot use the foreign supplier. And that ₹10 Cr is enough to put seven such chips into approved silicon. We are also asking you to accept a specific unfinished shape. The technology risk is mostly retired — there is silicon. The production risk is not. Nobody, including us, has taken a design made on a free kit through a full chip run and a dedicated mask set to an approved, listed part. That step is what this round buys, and that is the honest description of what ₹10 Cr is at risk against.

chunks.text: Every number behind those claims traces back to something you can look at: a timing report, a utilisation report, a signed purchase order, a scanned government list, or a generated circuit code file. DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL 14.2 Where we could fool ourselves — the audit we ran on our own plan We checked this plan for wishful thinking using investor Charlie Munger’s famous checklist — the way we would tear apart somebody else’s pitch. The core survives: the ten-times cost cut is arithmetic; ₹2.88 crore of orders is fact; the import bans are real. Four kinds of wishful thinking had crept in, and each one changed this document: • Borrowed glory. We quoted other companies’ huge order books in ways that made them sound like our orders. Fixed — they are labelled as the size of the door, and our money moves only on our own signed letters. • Permission mistaken for orders. A list entry is permission, not an order. Fixed — the three buyer speeds in §11.2, each with its own clock. • Protecting our own number. Our forecast added to exactly ₹1,000 crore in every revision — a sign we were protecting the number. Fixed — the crash-price table now travels with it everywhere. • One skill mistaken for another. Being good at chips is not being good at supporting three hundred customers. Fixed — the support-engineer team is a funded line. When everything pushes one way: national pride, government deadlines, finished docu- ments and exciting tender numbers all push the same direction — build more, faster. When every force in the room points one way, that is itself the warning. Our defence is the rule, the scoreboard, and the stop rules — written calmly, in advance. 15 What happens next Because a document should end with a step, not a summary. 1. A ninety-minute technical session, with the files open. Bring an engineer.

The fastest way through this document is to pick the claim you trust least and start there. 2. A data room, which is ready and does not wait on the round: the sky130 manufacturing files and the TinyTapeout 6 project, the generated processor circuit code, the FPGA timing and utilisation reports, the three signed customer contracts, the scanned government lists, and the source files that regenerate every drawing in this document. 3. The instrument, deliberately boring: a simple convertible, ₹10 Cr, capped below the institutional round, with the drone chip ring-fenced. 4. Two things we will send you without being asked, within sixty days, whether or not this progresses: the all-in cost of the 130 nm test chip, and the per-chip timing report. Those are the first two of the seven actions above. We would rather you judge us on whether they arrive than on whether we promised them. Aravind Prasad · Managing Director · aravind@deepgridsemi.com · +91 74163 19944 16 Word list Terms in the order a reader is likely to meet them. Term What it means 130 nm How small the smallest feature on the chip is. 130 nanometres is an older, larger, cheaper process. Newer phone chips are 3–5 nm. PDK, design kit The file set a factory gives you so you can design a chip for its process. Normally paid and under a non-disclosure agreement. sky130 and IHP’s are free. RTL, circuit code The code that describes what the chip does, before it becomes a physical layout. GDSII The final file the factory needs. It describes every shape on every layer of the chip. Physical design, layout Turning circuit code into actual shapes and wires. Normally sent to an outside company at $1–2 M per chip. Mask set The set of photographic stencils used to print the chip. A full set costs $0.5–1 M.
Term What it means MPW, shared factory run Several companies’ designs share one set of masks DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 70

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL and one wafer to split the cost. Cheap, but you only get about 100 chips. Wafer, wafer batch A 200 mm disc of silicon holding thousands of chips. A batch is 25 wafers. Yield The share of chips on a wafer that work. We assume 85 %. Die One individual chip, before it is packaged. QFN A common small chip package with pads underneath instead of legs. STA, timing analysis The check that proves a chip will work at its stated clock speed. FPGA A chip you can reprogram. Used to prove a design works before making a real chip. Slower than the real chip, which is why 81.25 MHz is not the product number. ASP Average selling price per chip. NRE Non-recurring engineering. The one-off setup cost before the first unit ships. AVL Approved-vendor list. Being on it means a buyer is allowed to purchase from you. PIL Positive Indigenisation List. A government list of items that may not be imported after a stated date. SRIJAN The government portal listing imported items that defence companies want replaced. DAP-2020 The defence procurement rules. Buy(Indian-IDDM) is the top priority category. Make-II A route where a successful trial earns a guaranteed order. MIL-883, JSS, CEMILAC Military testing and approval standards. Together they add 9–12 months. LRU Line-replaceable unit. A swappable box inside a vehicle or aircraft. DPSU Defence public-sector undertaking. A government-owned defence company, such as BEL or HAL. Analogue Circuits handling continuously varying signals, not just ones and zeros. Harder, slower to design, and needs silicon to verify. LDMOS, thick oxide Transistor types that survive high voltage. Available on older processes, not on newer ones. SiGe Silicon-germanium.

A material that makes much faster transistors, needed for 77 GHz radar. DICE latch, TMR Two ways of protecting stored data against cosmic-ray upsets. Both cost chip area. Lockstep Running two processors on the same program and comparing them, so a fault is caught immediately. PMP Physical memory protection. Keeps parts of the software separate from each other. Cache A small fast memory. Usually faster, but occasionally much slower, which is why our processors do not have one. SiP System in package. Several chips inside one package. KGD Known-good die. Testing each chip before assembly, so one bad chip does not ruin a package. Screened Individually tested to a military standard. Screened chips sell for 10–100 times the commercial price. Sources: the DeepGrid investor brief and SKU architecture compendium; the defence ministry’s 5th Positive Indigenisation List and DMA lists 1, 2, 3 and 5, read directly; UN COMTRADE HS 8542 for the import total; the generated DGridRiscV circuit code for §8; the ChipFoundry published shuttle schedule and price page and the EUROPRACTICE 2026 price list for §5 and §2, read on 4 August 2026. Volumes and prices are our own estimates unless a source is named. Performance curves in the drawings are example shapes against stated targets, not measurements. LOI (letter of intent) — a signed letter from a customer saying they intend to buy. Our gates open on these. Design-in — one customer engineering our chip into their product. Months of our support; five to ten per chip make its revenue. Crash case — the version of a forecast where things go badly. Ours sits beside the plan every- where the plan appears.

Stop rule — a decision written in advance — with a date — about what we do when a specific bad thing happens, so it cannot be renegotiated in an excited meeting. DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad 71

chunks.text: S K U - 5 Interface Transceiver — RS-485 + CAN-FD Thick-oxide 5 V LDMOS output stages · 30 mV hysteresis receivers · failsafe idle-recessive bias · ±15 kV HBM · line-timing budget shown. Replaces TI/ADI/Renesas interface parts — the classic obsolescence + FSC-5962 sourcing-bar wedge. 20–60M/yr attach-part volume: ships with every node on every bus. Why 130 nm wins here The sheet says it: a 5V-tolerant thick-oxide ring is exactly what a line driver wants — advanced nodes are actively worse for this part class. Status & node path Skew budget — not raw bitrate — sets node count and cable length; designed accordingly. ±CM per ISO 11898-2; HV bus-fault variant on SCL/IHP. Cycle-2 MPW. chunks.text: S K U - 6 Voltage Supervisor — Quad-Rail, Latched Fault Chopper-stabilised comparators · 0.1%-matched poly ladders · 8 µs deglitch · curvature-corrected bandgap 10 ppm/°C · windowed WDT. Replaces TI/Maxim supervisor sockets — 30–80M/yr attach volume, one or more on nearly every PCB; $0.2–0.8 ASP commercial, screened grades 10–100×. Qualification pathfinder Simplest die in the catalogue → first through MIL-883 — carries the screening flow for everything behind it while filling the highest-socket-count position (every LRU, every D100 module). Status & node path The deglitch counter is the design story: switching-noise immunity without slowing real fault response (<8 µs). sky130 → SCL. Cycle-1 or -2 MPW. chunks.section: 77 GHz MIMO Radar — SiGe Front End + CMOS Baseband
chunks.text: S K U - 7 77 GHz MIMO Radar — SiGe Front End + CMOS Baseband 2TX/4RX · IHP SG13G2 HBTs (ft 350 GHz) · 4 GHz sweep → 3.75 cm resolution · range/Doppler FFT + CFAR + beamforming on the CMOS die. The die boundary Stated on the sheet: ADC is the boundary — SiGe HBT die (chirp synth, PAs, 4 LNA/mixer/IF chains) + 130 nm CMOS die (12-bit 40 Msps ADCs, FFTs, CFAR, tracker). Gen-1 automotive partitioning. Socket & policy hook AD2 mirror-tower radar (captive) + defence perimeter/counter-UAS + automotive AEB — the only SKU with simultaneous captive automotive and defence sockets. Honesty on the sheet “The SiGe front end has no FPGA equivalent and is proven on silicon or not at all” — the risk statement is printed on the figure itself. IHP MPW FY28. chunks.text: S K U - 8 Rugged Display Driver — TFT Source Driver + TCON LVDS/DSI in · SXGA @ 60 Hz · 1280 × 10-bit column DACs · 0–12 V HV amps · temp-compensated gamma · frame-freeze BIST (ASIL-B capable). The policy anchor PIL-5 line item: BEL 17-inch rugged SXGA display, due Dec 2027 — a named DPSU socket with a date, cited from DDP's 5th list on the sheet itself. Replaces Novatek/Himax-class TCON + source-driver imports in defence MFDs, industrial HMI, rail PIS and automotive clusters — 2–6M/yr sockets at $3–12. Why 130 nm wins HV output amps (0–12 V swing, thick oxide) and 24 V gate-driver level shift are mature-node territory; charge-sharing precharge cuts driver power ~40%. Cycle-3 MPW. chunks.text: S K U - 9 SDV Zonal Controller + Gateway ASIL-D lockstep island · EVITA-full HSM + secure boot/OTA · TSN switch (802.1Qbv/AS) · CAN-FD×8, CAN-XL, LIN×8, FlexRay · smart fuse ×16. Scope honesty (on-sheet) 130 nm at 200 MHz owns the ZONAL layer — gateway, smart I/O, safety and security edge. Central SDV compute (multi-GHz, GPU/NPU, LPDDR5) is sub-10 nm and explicitly NOT claimed. Socket & market 4–12M/yr India zonal sockets at $6–20 as OEMs replace relay-and-harness architectures; ~$0.3–0.7B addressable, zonal layer only — flagged internal estimate. Where it fits Bridges the CV ADAS heritage (AD2) and the DG SDV platform: this is the mature-node edge of the same architecture Design.png shows at the centre. chunks.docTitle: Technical Annex v3 (10 SKUs, D100 & SDV)
chunks.text: D 1 0 0 Drone SoC D100 — Phase 2, the Revenue-Now Silicon Flight control (PX4/ArduPilot loop) + visual-inertial odometry (EKF pose 30 Hz) + optional 10-TOPS NPU — with a hardware failsafe island independent of the mission stack. The wedge (on-sheet) Failsafe island in hardware, not firmware: link monitor → safe-state FSM → independent path direct to ESC, isolated power and clock — bypasses FC, VIO and AI. DGCA type-certification path. Market (sheet, cited) India drone market $1.2–1.3B → $2.7–3.2B by ’30–34; SoC ASP $100–800; ideaForge guided 340–450 units in Q4 FY26 alone. No indigenous FC+VIO SoC exists — gap stated with references. Status FPGA prototype validates; product is 130 nm at 200 MHz fixed. VIO is geometry, not learned perception — survives GPS jamming (LoC/LAC use case). Deepgrid Semi · SKU Architecture Compendium v3 · Annex to Investor Brief · 2026 · Confidential

chunks.docTitle: Technical Annex v3 (10 SKUs, D100 & SDV)
chunks.text: T R A C K B DG SDV Platform — The Architecture Behind It All Deepgrid’s platform reference: secure + safe (triple-lockstep) + Linux host (RV64GCH) + vector & integer accelerator domains on a 64-bit AXI4 matrix with AXI-REALM QoS. SKU-9 is the mature-node zonal edge of this platform; the D100 is its airborne sibling; SKU-3 powers, SKU-6 supervises, SKU-5 connects — one architecture, many dies. chunks.text: S i P SiP Integration — How the Dies Compose Wire-bonded mature dies + one flip-chip 28 nm compute die on a 4-layer organic substrate — mature-node packaging at mature-node cost. Package summary 4-layer organic substrate · BGA 15×15 · wire-bond ×6 + flip-chip ×1 · die-to-die SPI/UART/GPIO over substrate · power tree from SKU-3 · SKU-6 supervises the package · deliberately not UCIe. Wave 2 The 28 nm AI-compute die (D100 core) joins after the ₹50 Cr round — same substrate, same supervision, one SDV/UAV module. chunks.docTitle: Technical Annex v3 (10 SKUs, D100 & SDV)
chunks.text: R O A D M A P Node & SKU Roadmap — Three Phases, Arithmetic-Checked 130/180 nm ships the catalogue; 90/55/45 nm takes the logic-bound parts from 2028; 28 nm takes compute from 2030 — with the honest boundary and the SKU-ramp correction printed on the figure. Phase 2 · why shrink at all Channel count and DSP throughput — not speed vanity: GNSS baseband (90/55), SDR transceiver (SiGe+CMOS), drone nav co-processor (55/45). Analog IO rings stay 130 nm where voltage and ESD demand it. Phase 3 · the honest boundary “Everything above is a sub-10 nm problem. 28 nm buys some of it. None of it is claimable on 130 nm, at any clock.” — printed on the roadmap itself. The arithmetic check The figure corrects its own draft: 10 SKUs/yr and 1,000 SKUs by Year 5 were inconsistent by 20×. Shown ramp: ~50-SKU catalogue by Year 5 — one number, before an investor finds two. Deepgrid Semi · SKU Architecture Compendium v3 · Annex to Investor Brief · 2026 · Confidential
